articles.title_orig: Live updates: Zelensky warns Putin poses global danger as Iran’s president strikes defiant tone at UN
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Zelensky warns Putin poses global danger as Iran’s president strikes defiant tone at UN
articles.content_orig:
• Iran president speaks: In his UNGA address, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will not bend to US President Donald Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” A US delegate in the room walked out.
• No breakthrough: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that US-Iran mediated talks on the sidelines of UNGA did not yield any major breakthrough, indicating the memorandum of understanding from earlier this year was no longer in the cards.
• Zelensky delivers remarks: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” saying the Russian leader spreads war and instability. As he spoke, Zelensky’s party headquarters were struck by Russia, according to Kyiv officials.
• Eyes on Venezuela: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez will address UNGA more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, who is currently being held in a Brooklyn detention center. Trump met with her last night as Washington maintains political pressure on Venezuela to enact reforms.
Zelensky's party headquarters in Kyiv was struck as he spoke at UNGA
A convention center that hosts the party headquarters of Volodymyr Zelensky was hit in a Russian attack as the Ukrainian leader addressed the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, according to Kyiv city officials.
The strike was the latest in a string of attacks on the country that took place throughout the day.
Attacks in Kyiv killed two people and injured 43 others, city officials said. Among the strikes was one near a university and two on the convention center — the second of which took place as Zelensky spoke.
The roof of the convention center was damaged and the fire resulting from the attack was put out, emergency services said.
Heavy explosions were also heard overnight in the Ukrainian capital, with the air force reporting numerous ballistic missiles in the sky.
Russian forces also dropped four aerial bombs on the Ukrainian village of Oleksandrivka in the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine on Wednesday morning, killing at least five people, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin.
At least six people were reported injured in the bombing, and seven others, including two children, are believed to be trapped under rubble following the morning attack, Filashkin posted to Telegram.
At least 12 apartment buildings, 42 private homes, an administrative building, a kindergarten, a shop and seven vehicles were damaged, he said, adding that search and rescue efforts are ongoing.
Trump and first lady greet Xi as Chinese leader arrives in US
President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greeted Chinese President Xi Jinping and Madame Peng Liyuan at Joint Base Andrews Wednesday evening, participating in a brief arrival ceremony.
Xi walked down the steps of his aircraft at 6:02 p.m. EST alongside his wife, where the Trumps were waiting to receive them on a 100-foot-long red carpet.
They shook hands and exchanged words for a few minutes through a translator. Xi was given a bouquet of flowers which he quickly passed off to a staffer.
This is the first time Xi has visited Washington, DC, since 2015. Trump traveled to China for a series of events with Xi in May.
The arrival ceremony included ceremonial cannon volleys, a 21-person honor cordon, two three-person color teams with both the US and Chinese flags, the US Air Force Band, playing the US and Chinese National Anthems and two B1 flyovers.
Yemen vice president says country's government needs clear US support
The Vice President of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Dr. Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir said the Yemeni government needs clear US support amid gains by the Houthis.
“The Yemeni people are actually capable and determined to go through with their confrontation of the Houthis,” Al-Alimi told reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
He called for US military and security support, saying it was “a contribution not just to keep Yemen safe, but also in order to keep the region and the whole world safe.” He said such support could be in the form of training or weapons.
The Iranian-backed Houthis have captured swaths of the Red Sea coastline, threatening open access to the critical Bab al Mandeb waterway, and have also launched strikes targeting Saudi energy infrastructure as the war in Iran is poised to escalate onto another front.
Yemeni President Rashad Al-Alimi spoke in recent days with US President Donald Trump, the vice president said. He did not say what Trump agreed to provide, but said he was “not aware” that Trump declined a request for assistance.
He repeatedly said he was confident the US understood the threat posed by the Houthis and voiced appreciation for US actions like its military strikes last year and its designation of the group as a foreign terrorist organization.
The Trump administration, for now, has drawn a line at kinetic strikes against the Houthis and instead has provided Saudi Arabia with additional intelligence and targeting information.
Venezuela's National Assembly expresses support for Delcy Rodríguez's trip to the UN
Venezuela’s National Assembly, where the ruling United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV) holds the majority, approved an agreement today, backing acting President Delcy Rodríguez’s trip to the United Nations General Assembly.
The expression of support was approved during a session of the legislative body, according to its president, Jorge Rodríguez, the acting president’s brother.
The National Assembly’s support comes after opposition groups and several citizens rejected the acting president’s trip.
She took office following the capture of President Nicolás Maduro in early January during a U.S. military operation, and many consider her an illegitimate ruler.
The acting Venezuelan president is scheduled to address the UN General Assembly tonight.
During her stay in New York, Rodríguez has also met with several world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, Trinidad and Tobago Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar and the Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten. She is scheduled to meet with Chilean President José Antonio ahead of her address.
Why some Venezuelans reject Delcy Rodríguez’s participation in UNGA
Some Venezuelan citizens have rejected acting President Delcy Rodríguez’s trip to the United Nations ahead of her remarks today at the General Assembly.
Rodríguez became acting president in early January after the US captured President Nicolás Maduro in a military operation. He is being held in New York on various charges, which he denies.
Rodríguez initially criticized Maduro’s arrest but has since had various dealings with the Trump administration, including an agreement for the US to control 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil.
Protester Margot Monasterios said Venezuelans are “grateful” to Trump for ousting Maduro but noted that key figures from his inner circle remain in power.
Away from the protest, other citizens shared similar opinions. “We’ve really had it up to here with this government, honestly,” Mary Romero said.
Meanwhile, Rafael Azuaje said, “(Rodríguez) was not elected by the will of the people. Second, she shouldn’t be there because what they did was deceive the Venezuelan people, taking away all the mineral wealth, while the people are actually even worse off.”
What to know about Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s leader after Maduro’s capture by US
Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly later, on the second day of its 81st session.
In January, US President Donald Trump announced the US military had carried out a large-scale military operation to capture and arrest Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Delcy Rodríguez then became the interim president of the country.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Treasury rates spiked on Wednesday to multiyear highs in what was the biggest one-day move for the 10-year Treasury yield in nearly 18 months. There were a number of reasons cited for the sudden move higher:
- Much stronger-than-expected surveys on U.S. economic activity, especially in the manufacturing sector
- Hawkish commentary from a top Federal Reserve official
- A U.S. Treasury auction for five-year notes that was met with poor demand
- Stubbornly high oil prices with WTI crude rising 2%
The 10-year Treasury note yield popped more than 13 basis points to 5.104% and reached a level not seen since July 2007. The move gained steam after the 10-year yield broke through the key 5% level. It marked the benchmark yield's biggest one-day move since April 7, 2025 — when it surged 16.6 points.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, which is most sensitive to expected changes in Fed policy, jumped more than 11 basis points to 4.889% and hit its highest level since May 2024 as traders increased their bet the Federal Reserve would need to hike again in October.
The 30-year Treasury yield gained more than 9 basis points to 5.398%. It hit the highest level since June 2007. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
"This is the market telling us we've entered a genuine re-tightening cycle, said Tony Miano, global investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. "The Fed's 25 basis point hike last week to 3.75%–4% was its first increase since 2023, and the dot plot signaled another this year."
"A week ago you could argue that was a one-and-done insurance move or a one and maybe December hike). Today's price action says investors no longer believe that," he added. Bottom line, "you can't fool or hide in the bond market – unless the Fed gets inflation under control the long end of the curve is going to continue to come under pressure."
Purchasing managers' indexes are typically not huge market movers, but Wednesday morning's readings from S&P Global caught the market off guard. The firm's services PMI jumped to 58.7 in September, its highest level in nearly five years, from 56.5 in August. Its manufacturing counterpart raced to 56.7, a level not seen in more than four years. PMIs are surveys of managers in different sectors across the economy.
"US business continues to boom," S&P Global Market Intelligence chief business economist Chris Williamson said in a statement. "To put the growth surge in context, barring the spike in demand following the opening up of the economy after the COVID-19 lockdowns, the latest improvement in business activity is the greatest recorded since early 2015. Business is clearly booming now in both manufacturing and services."
"Input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher thanks to the rise in oil prices," he added.
Barr's warning, poor auction
Comments from Fed Governor Michael Barr then added even more upward pressure to yields.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," said Barr. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that."
Following the first Fed rate hike in more than years last week, odds of another quarter-point rate increase in October rose Wednesday to 66.4% from 55% a day before, per the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Those chances stood at less than 10% a month ago.
Traders also contended with a much weaker-than-expected Treasury Department auction of 5-year notes. According to BMO, the sale concluded with a yield of 5.033% — far above a six-auction average of 4.186%. Indirect bidders, which include global central banks, scooped up 54% of the auction, well below a 65% average.
"Bottom line, a poor auction with Treasury trying to sell paper into a weak market and where yields weren't attractive enough to bring in the buyers," Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, wrote in a Wednesday note. "The bond bear market continues on."
At the heart of the move higher in yields are persistently higher oil prices. Brent futures rallied 3.86% to settle at $103.08 per barrel, while U.S. crude gained 1.81% to settle at $92.16 per barrel.
Oil prices have been soaring this year as the U.S.-Iran war continues, sparking fears of sticky inflation — which may lead to more Fed rate hikes.

articles.title_zh: NRSC Chair Tim Scott leaves Georgia, North Carolina off his list of top Senate targets
articles.content_orig:
The GOP’s Incredible Shrinking Senate Map
Trump has so badly damaged the Republican Party’s brand that strategists are contemplating bitter fights—and losses—in races they’d been banking on as sure things.
If you obsessively read or write about politics, you’ve probably lost track of the number of times that political reporters happened upon major-party operatives in “panic mode.” Just this week, Democrats were said to be sounding an “alarm” because of a single poll in the New Hampshire open-seat Senate race showing a dead heat. But the struggle ahead for the GOP this year more than justifies the panic framing. Republican strategists are starting to see the birds head out to sea and the faint outline of an inbound tsunami. When the wave hits in early November, Republican Senate candidates—even in deep-red states like South Carolina, Kansas, and Florida—could be frantically bailing their way out before a Democratic surge without precedent in the past two decades.
Media attention to this development is overly focused on individual polls. And yes, there have been a handful of eyebrow-raising Senate surveys showing Democratic candidates like Florida’s Angie Nixon running even with their opponents in Republican strongholds. But Democrats are dreaming about these races not just because they’re high on hopium and a smattering of polls show their candidates within striking distance of a win. They’re taking their cues from broader structural shifts in the national political environment.
If recent polls are to be believed, this could be, in raw popular vote totals, the biggest blowout national election of the 21st century—one that has at least a chance of delivering the kind of victory Democrats have spent more than a decade hoping for. Last week, the comparatively staid New York Times/Siena College poll pegged the Democrats lead on the generic ballot at nearly nine points. Remember that in the two big GOP midterm waves of this century—2010 and 2014—Republicans won the national House popular vote by 6.8 and 5.7 points, respectively. The Democratic wave of 2018 was 8.6 points, the high-water mark for any midterm election this century.
Neither party has won a double-digit popular vote victory in a midterm election since Democrats in 1982, halfway through Ronald Reagan’s first term. But this pattern looks very much like it could change this year. In data guru Nate Silver’s generic ballot model, Democrats have opened up their biggest lead of the cycle at 8.6 points.
And there’s still worse news for Republicans: The GOP’s average reading in this measure is down since the spring—a sign of real erosion in support that lines up with the big drop in President Trump’s approval rating over the same period. Given this overall trend, there’s also ample space and time for the Democratic lead to grow—especially in light of the president’s apparent determination to inflict as much damage on his own party as possible. When you get past a 10-point lead on the generic ballot—which a number of surveys already show happening—the firewalls start to break.
The reasons for Democrats’ optimism are not a mystery. The president spent 2025 burning through his political capital on a nationwide ICE reign of terror, an indiscriminate slash-and-burn evisceration of the federal government, a slapdash tariff war, and an orgy of unapologetic self-dealing that would make Mobutu Sese Seko blush. Trump’s record was so bad that a record number of Democrats had emerged as favorites to claim a House majority by the end of last year. At that point, Trump maintained a high enough approval rating to make GOP control of the Senate a near-certainty. What’s more, the economy was growing, the stock market booming, and inflation within range of stability—all traditionally encouraging metrics for the party in power in Washington.
Then came 2026. The year started with an embarrassing effort to use the DOJ to scrub Trump’s involvement in the notorious international sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein’s files—one of many own-goals the president has scored on himself since taking office again. Having spent a decade railing against “forever wars” in the Middle East, Trump then made the inexplicable decision to attempt a decapitation of the Iranian government. The caper has gone so badly that it has single-handedly given the country’s autocrats a new lease on life, made the entire US strategic position in the Middle East look untenable, and triggered a cascading global economic crisis.
Not content to suffer this brutal but politically survivable humiliation, Trump has elected not to take any of the many off-ramps that have been offered to him. Even now, he could relieve some of the electoral pressure on his congressional lickspittles by simply allowing Iran to control the Strait of Hormuz, which would begin the long process of bringing down energy prices. But Trump is so profoundly vain and ignorant that he just can’t bring himself to do it, since a climbdown in Hormuz would involve at least an implicit acknowledgement that the war was a terrible mistake.
Now with bond markets in turmoil, the stock market declining, interest rates rising to get the Iran-driven inflation disaster under control, and spiking energy prices that may tip multiple countries into complete social mayhem, Trump keeps firing off the dumbest remarks imaginable. On Wednesday, he called skyrocketing gas prices a “very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done” in Iran—a few months after declaring that he wasn’t “thinking at all” about the finances of Americans as he prosecuted the war. He’s doing the job of Democratic ad-makers for them.
On top of all this, the president is stumbling around like a blackout drunk picking fights with anyone he runs into, up to and including our historically mild-mannered northern neighbor Canada. To put a flourish on his rudderless megalomania, he continues to campaign to rename things after himself or America—and when it looks like he may not get his way, to threaten their demolition. If you sat down and came up with a 10-point plan to alienate unaffiliated and Republican-leaning independents as thoroughly as possible, you couldn’t do better than this.
What’s the upshot of all of this madness? Democrats have already gone from longshots to betting favorites in enough Senate races to take back the majority. In Ohio, Texas, and Alaska, Democratic candidates have taken the lead, with top-line numbers high enough for party leaders to be reasonably confident that undecided voters can’t save the day for the MAGA right by breaking for the Republican candidate at the 11th hour. All three states voted for Trump by double digits in 2024, and a loss in any of those three races would have been seen as a catastrophe by Republicans a year ago. Today, they would probably feel fortunate to win any one of the three—to say nothing of Iowa, where Nate Silver’s model gives Democrat Josh Turek a 44 percent chance of prevailing.
But the fallout from what is easily the most catastrophic policy year overseen by any US president since 2008 may drift further downwind than that. Take South Carolina. Six years ago, Democrat Jaime Harrison came within 10 points of unseating the late Lindsey Graham, in a year where Democrats carried the House popular vote by just 3.1 points. Over the summer, when Graham died suddenly, Trump made the baffling decision to strongarm South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster into appointing Graham’s sister Darline Graham Nordone to the seat. With Trump’s backing, she won the August primary for the seat despite a series of embarrassing campaign gaffes.

All eyes in the college football world will be on Knoxville for Week 4, with another epic SEC showdown on the schedule with the No. 1-ranked Texas Longhorns heading to Neyland Stadium for a showdown with the No. 14 Tennessee Volunteers. On Wednesday, we learned that President Donald Trump will be in attendance.
ESPN will also be on the scene for College GameDay, marking the second time this month that the Longhorns are featured on the premier college football pre-game show. College GameDay was previously in Austin ahead of Texas' epic comeback win over Ohio State.
With College GameDay and Trump in town at the same town, fans immediately started questioning whether he will be making an appearance on ESPN during the pre-game festivities.
WATCH: Ted Cruz ruthlessly booed on College GameDay while promoting Protect College Sports Act
Whether it be for a segment a la the poorly received Ted Cruz-Save College Sports Act segment that was ruthlessly booed in Austin or as a celebrity guest picker, many wonder whether the president will make a cameo.
The ESPN College GameDay TV setup is seen in The Grove in Oxford, Miss., on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. Credit: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
CBS Sports revealed that ESPN declined comment on whether Trump will make an appearance, so everything remains up in the air just a few days until showtime.
What we do know, however, is that each fan bases will be hoping to avoid the Trump curse, with his recent poor track record of publicly backing teams and players.
Kickoff between the top-ranked Longhorns and No. 14 Volunteers at Neyland Stadium is set for 12:00 p.m. ET on ABC. All of the information you need to catch Saturday afternoon's SEC showdown can be seen below.

articles.title_orig: Giants QB Jaxson Dart will have knee surgery, ending his 2026 season
articles.title_zh: Giants QB Jaxson Dart will have knee surgery, ending his 2026 season
articles.content_orig:
Jaxson Dart's season is over.
The New York Giatns quarterback will undergo surgery and land on injured reserve after getting hurt during Monday night's 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, head coach John Harbaugh announced. While Dart is expected to make a full recovery, his 2026 season will be over.
According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, Dart's injury includes damage to his left MCL, PCL and meniscus. There is reportedly no ACL damage.
Harbaugh met with reporters on Tuesday afternoon and said that Dart was continuing to be evaluated and they had not made any decisions on the quarterback's status. The team "learned a lot more" about the injury following the MRI.
Harbaugh confirmed the injury on Wednesday afternoon. He did stop short of ruling Dart out for the postseason, should the Giants make the playoffs, but Dart will have surgery in the near future.
Dart suffered the injury in the first quarter on Monday night and did not return to the game. X-rays were negative and the second-year signal-caller underwent an MRI on Tuesday after the team returned home from Los Angeles.
During the game's opening drive, Dart dropped back to pass and jumped to make a throw downfield while under pressure. He was sandwiched between Rams linebackers Josaiah Stewart and Byron Young before falling to the ground holding his left knee.
Jaxson Dart is down on the field after this play. pic.twitter.com/R059M6kM6e
— TSN (@TSN_Sports) September 22, 2026
After being tended to on the field, Dart limped off and was taken for further evaluation. He was initially listed as questionable to return before being ruled out. He returned later without his uniform and watched the remainder of the game from the sideline.
Jameis Winston, who signed a two-year, $13-million extension before Week 1, finished the game going 11-for-27 with 111 passing yards, an interception and taking two sacks. Now, with Dart out for the year, Winston will presumably take the reins the rest of the way.
Jaxson Dart among Giants' MNF injury concerns
Dart wasn't the only injured Giant coming out of Monday night.
Wide receiver Malik Nabers injured his right shoulder in the first quarter. Nabers told reporters afterward that the shoulder popped out and he popped it back in, allowing him to return to the game the next series.
Linebacker Brian Burns had his left ankle rolled on by a Rams offensive lineman and needed help getting off the field. He limped his way to the Giants' locker room and was diagnosed with a low ankle sprain. He reportedly wore a boot on his left foot and while he said it's "nothing serious," it's unclear if Burns will miss any time.
Left tackle Andrew Thomas suffered a groin injury on the team's final offensive play, but no update has been provided on his status.
The Giants entered the game without cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo, who were ruled out due to injury.
The Giants' next two games are at home against the Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals. They will go back on the road for Week 5 to face the Washington Commanders and return home for Week 6 against the New Orleans Saints. They will then travel to take on the Houston Texans before their bye in Week 8.

articles.title_orig: Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
articles.title_zh: Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
articles.content_orig:
Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
Clavicular, the controversial streamer who rose from the corners of the internet to the mainstream advocating for extreme tactics to achieve physical attractiveness, now finds his internet fame spilling into the courtroom.
Braden Peters, better known for his online moniker, has been charged in Massachusetts court with rape, drugging a person for sex and providing alcohol to an underage person, court records show.
Peters, 20, has become the visible face of the "looksmaxxing" movement. He’s gone to extremes such as hitting himself in the face with a hammer so his bones supposedly grow back sharper and taking small amounts of methamphetamine in an attempt to suppress his appetite. Offshoots of the trend, which are associated with the "manosphere," have ventured into sexist, misogynistic and racist philosophies, while Peters himself has drawn criticism for using racial slurs during his streams.
The viral nature of his controversial soundbites and short-form content helped usher what was once a niche subculture on obscure Reddit forums into the mainstream on TikTok, Instagram and Kik, where he’s collectively amassed more than 2.7 million followers. Now, the turn in his trajectory offers a window into the pitfalls of a movement drawing young men online in droves.
What is 'looksmaxxing,' the 'manosphere?'
"Looksmaxxing" is the process of maximizing one’s physical appearance through hygiene, fitness and style.
The term has gone mainstream and can have positive implications, such as getting healthy or working out more in the hopes of finding more confidence in the dating world.
However, the looksmaxxing movement has roots in online incel culture, which villainizes women, and has become a new subset of the "manosphere," a digital collection of websites, videos and social media that promote male supremacy and advocate for traditional gender roles.
How young men get sucked into 'looksmaxxing'
The combination of technology and the natural insecurities that arise during teenage years creates a "perfect storm" for innocuous sports and health spaces to tune young men into radical content, Gary Barker, the president of Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, an organization that advocates for healthy manhood, previously told USA TODAY.
"They’re going there with kind of innocent intentions, but without somebody else supporting them, that innocent intention can become a follower who drops their critical thinking," Barker said.
Looksmaxxing creators have become a modern extension for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Among these creators, such as Kareem Shami, an early adopter who encourages "mewing," and Alex Costa, who focuses on "softmaxxing" with style and haircare, Clavicular has become the most extreme, advocating for surgical upgrades. In June, he livestreamed his rhinoplasty on Kick, undergoing four procedures ahead of Paris Fashion Week in what he called "Ascension Week."
As his looksmaxxing tactics have been more extreme, so have his far-right, sexist and racist rhetoric.
His streams often feature degrading language regarding women, and he was seen partying in Miami with Andrew and Tristan Tate, manosphere creator Sneako and far-right nationalist Nick Fuentes in January, where the group was filmed singing along to Ye’s "Heil Hitler."
On Sept. 4, Romanian prosecutors indicted 39-year-old Andrew Tate for allegedly trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering, and his 38-year-old brother Tristan Tate for alleged complicity.
"The current version of the manosphere has become much more mainstream than it used to be," said University of Wisconsin-Madison public affairs professor Mariel Barnes, whose research focuses on backlash to gender equality and the manosphere. "You don't need to hide who you are anymore if you're a raging misogynist."
Extreme fringes of the manosphere have orchestrated or praised violent attacks against women, a trend Netflix’s 2025 crime drama "Adolescence" highlighted by following the story of a 13-year-old boy who was radicalized by misogynistic culture online.
Peters' September charges come after his teen protege Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza sued him in April for physical and sexual abuse after an incident at his Cape Cod, Massachusetts, home in May 2025. Mendoza alleged that the content creator had sex with her while she was intoxicated and without consent, and injected her with an "unapproved drug" during a livestream when she was 16.
Young men who tune into extreme content and are isolated from women and other men are more likely to take on radical views or engage in violence, according to Barnes.
"If you are constantly consuming this content and you are isolated and women are responsible for the bad things that are happening to you, it's very dehumanizing, right?" Barnes said. "You don't see women as humans anymore, or as peers or as friends, and that dehumanization gives you permission to treat them as less than human."

articles.title_orig: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.title_zh: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price tags (thanks RAMageddon!).
Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
The Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch both have better battery life and performance, but higher price tags.
While the 12-inch Surface Pro started at $799.99 last year, it’s debuting on October 13th at a starting price of $1,149.99. Likewise, the 13-inch Surface Laptop was originally priced at $899.99, but it’s up to $1,199.99 this time around. There’s no base 8GB model this time, causing some of the price increase, as both devices launch with a minimum of 16GB of RAM and can be configured up to 24GB.
Pricing aside, Microsoft is promising that the six-core Snapdragon X2 Plus chips will deliver up to 18 percent more efficient battery performance, more than 60 percent faster graphics performance, and up to 95 percent faster local AI inferencing on the built-in NPU.
That’s a lot of percentages, but what it equates to on these devices is better battery life and improved performance. On the Surface Pro 12-inch Second Edition, as Microsoft calls it, that means an extra hour of web browsing (up to 13 hours in total), and on the Surface Laptop 13-inch Second Edition it’s two extra hours of web browsing usage (up to 18 hours in total).
Microsoft is using similar displays on these models as last year, so the Surface Pro 12-inch has a 2196 x 1464 (220 PPI) LCD display that runs at up to 90Hz. The Surface Laptop 13-inch still ships with a 1920 x 1280 (178 PPI) display that only runs at 60Hz. Both displays have been upgraded from 400 nits of brightness to 500 nits, though.
Port selection remains the same, too. Both devices include two USB-C 3.2 ports, and the Surface Laptop 13-inch also has a USB-A 3.2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Both also support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity.
I’m surprised that Microsoft hasn’t upgraded at least one of these smaller Surface devices with a haptic trackpad, particularly because Windows 11 now adds subtle haptic nudges, and the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with haptic feedback. Microsoft is launching a second edition of its Surface Mouse with integrated haptics, and you can read all about that here.
Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both devices will also be sold to commercial customers, and the Surface Pro 12-inch will be available in an optional 5G configuration.

articles.content_orig:
Dolly Parton's Manager Accuses Singer's Nephew of Violent Threats, 'I'm a Killer'
Dolly Parton's Manager Files For Restraining Order Against Her Nephew Alleges 'Killer' Threats, Intimidation
Dolly Parton's family war is getting ugly ... with her longtime manager filing a lawsuit seeking a temporary restraining order against the late singer's nephew, Bryan Seaver, TMZ has learned.
TMZ obtained court docs filed by Dolly's manager, Danny Nozell. The manager claims Bryan began "invoking his self-proclaimed military-contractor experience, access to weapons, and capacity for violence" to extort Dolly's manager into giving in to his demands for money.
The manager said he was forced to terminate Bryan due to his threatening conduct ... and said he started a campaign of threats, intimidation, and coercion a few weeks before her passing.
One alleged threat read, "Her money better be bigger than I can make elsewhere or I'm going to f*** everyone. I am about to become the hand of retribution for my entire family."
Another alleged threat sent by Bryan read, "I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnership and telling the violations these people have done on us."
Another alleged message read, "All I do is warfare ... everyone needs to be worried about what I might do." Seaver also allegedly wrote "I'm not an entertainment person. I'm a killer" and "I'm going to ratf**k every entity I can possibly conjure" in messages submitted as exhibits.
The manager terminated Bryan on September 15. His lawsuit is asking for Bryan to not interfere with Dolly's business and leave their business partners alone ... and stay 1,000 feet away from the offices.
As TMZ first reported, Seaver was recently kicked off her properties after working as her head of security for years.
Bryan denies the claims in the petition. He tells TMZ ... "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."
He added, "However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by." Bryan said the messages were taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.
"I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster," he said. "A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."
In regard to the "rat f**k" comment, Bryan tells us "I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that."
Dolly died on August 25, 2026, at the age of 80 ... and Bryan himself announced via her Instagram.

articles.title_orig: Seahawks' Macdonald apologizes to Broncos' Payton for comments
articles.title_zh: Seahawks' Macdonald apologizes to Broncos' Payton for comments
articles.content_orig:
Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald told reporters Wednesday that the viral story he shared about Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton accusing the Seahawks of cheating during the 2024 season wasn't intended for public use.
The 39-year-old Macdonald, now in his third season at the helm in Seattle, said he apologized to Payton for the Graham Bensinger interview clip.
Macdonald also acknowledged that he's "got to be better in that moment" and remember that he's always responsible for his words, regardless of the situation.
#Seahawks HC Mike Macdonald says he called Broncos HC Sean Payton to apologize after his Spygate story went public (when it was meant to remain private):
“It’s a lesson learned. … I’m responsible for what I say.” https://t.co/8oT85eFIFE pic.twitter.com/Ud2B10xojP
In the clip, which circulated widely across social media on Tuesday, Macdonald divulged how, long after the Seahawks defeated the Broncos 26-20 in Macdonald's first-ever regular-season game as a head coach back in 2024, Payton "basically threatened to come out publicly and do a whole Patriot Spygate type of thing."
Payton eventually heard that Macdonald and his staff had gathered an assortment of Broncos plays Denver fans had recorded during training camp practice and posted to social media, Macdonald explained to Bensinger. Macdonald said that, since those videos were public, Seattle used them to its advantage, scouting every one of them before the season opener. That methodology isn't unheard of in today's NFL.
Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley revealed earlier this month that, when he hired former Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo, he discovered that Patullo had "half" of Hafley's pressures on tape from fans videoing Green Bay Packers training camp in the lead-up to the 2024 campaign, Hafley's first as Packers defensive coordinator. Hafley noted he deployed a pressure in that season's opener that he had never run, "and they knew it was coming," and "[Patullo] said he saw that pressure on video." The Eagles won that Week 1 game 34-29 in Brazil.
As for Payton's suspicions, Macdonald said the renowned offensive coach called Seahawks general manager John Schneider and, according to Macdonald, expressed that he "thought it was a Michigan thing where we had a plant and the whole thing."
Macdonald continued: "So we had to counter with him to say like, 'Hey, look, if you come out of this, we're going to sue you because it's not true.'"
Payton ultimately let it go, Macdonald said.
He then added: "It was like the Cold War. [Payton] was like, 'I'm going to hit the button. I'm going to hit the button.' [We were like,] 'No, we're going to hit the button.' So none of us hit the button."
That candid exchange between Macdonald and Bensinger took place on set where the rest of the interview apparently occurred; however, it seemed as though Macdonald was especially relaxed and informal in the way he was telling the tale. The clip's camera angle was notably unorthodox as well, with the mic and lighting fixtures in view.
When asked Wednesday if he thought he was simply shooting the breeze with Bensinger before the cameras were rolling, Macdonald said, "Yeah."
"It's something that I didn't intend for public use," Macdonald said earlier in his news conference, "but it just felt like it was the most appropriate thing to reach out to Sean and really just apologize to him for having that end up be public where it wasn't meant to.
"It's something that [the Broncos] have to deal with in real time that wasn't really on their end. So that's really where you're like, 'Crap.' But it's a lesson learned."
He went on: "Honestly, I got to be better in that moment for understanding like, look, I'm responsible for what I say really no matter the circumstance, whether you're mic'd up, whether you're not, whether you have a certain type of understanding. So I fell short in that moment. So it stings for me, frankly, but it's something that I'm definitely going to learn from. And just a good example that we just got to take responsibility for the things that we say."
Macdonald conveyed that Payton was gracious in his response to the apology.
"Sean was great," Macdonald said. "I respect the heck out of him and his program, always have. He's a phenomenal football coach. It's been great to get to know him at the owners meetings the last couple years, and he was awesome.
"So I know we're both looking forward to moving forward from it, but I really appreciate how he handled it."
Payton: 'He and I are good'
Payton, a Super Bowl-winning coach like Macdonald, confirmed the two spoke Tuesday night.
"He and I are good," Payton said at his Wednesday news conference. "Lord knows, I've been in his position where you're talking about something ... and the story is three years ago. Now, I don't know Mike at that time really, but I know Schneides really well. And, so, I'm sure my initial call to John wasn't pleasant, but I would say this, in talking with him, it allowed us to figure out how to handle our training camp relative to just videos.
"And I don't think anything was intentional by fans. You know what I mean? But at first, you're kind of thinking, man, how could … ? And then we did some research online of what was available, and that's kind of how we changed our policy."
So, in that way, the whole kerfuffle actually helped the Broncos "to some degree," Payton said.
A reporter inquired if Payton originally thought the Seahawks taped Denver's plays, not fans. He conceded he didn't know back then.
"So obviously I called shooting before I started looking. And I could only do that with John because, again, he's someone I'll have a beer with at the [NFL] combine. I consider him a good friend. But it was eye-opening relative to just, 'Alright, we got to be better in this area.'"
Payton went as far to say that Denver's pulling for Macdonald's Seahawks, "except for one game" (the teams will face off on "Thursday Night Football" in Week 6). After all, Seattle's playing the AFC West this season, so it could hand the Broncos' three divisional foes losses.
"Like I said, the conversation last night was good," Payton said, alluding to his talk with Macdonald. "I have a ton of respect for him, and that's it."

articles.title_orig: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.title_zh: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.
In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US.
But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.
A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.
The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar.
He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.
Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons.
He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.
Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.”
He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”.
Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.
He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

articles.title_orig: Trump ready to ban diesel gas exports to lower costs at home – something his own energy secretary says could backfire
articles.title_zh: Trump ready to ban diesel gas exports to lower costs at home – something his own energy secretary says could backfire
articles.content_orig:
Trump ready to ban diesel gas exports to lower costs at home – something his own energy secretary says could backfire
If implemented, it would be the first restriction on American energy exports in over a decade
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Donald Trump is preparing to institute a 90-day ban on diesel exports in a bid to bring down soaring prices — despite opposition from Energy Secretary Chris Wright and industry insiders, according to a new report.
The prohibition, which would be the first restriction on American energy exports in over a decade, could be announced in the coming days, Politico reported. The hope among administration officials is that, by redirecting diesel bound for Asia or Europe back into the U.S., it could provide relief at the pump ahead of the midterm elections. The White House described the story as “fake news.”
Global energy prices have risen dramatically amid the ongoing Iran war, largely due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical trade route. On Wednesday, the average national price for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.52, up from $3.69 one year ago, according to AAA.
A number of top officials, including Wright and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, as well as oil industry executives, have balked at the possibility of a 90-day ban.
“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work because the U.S. exports a lot of diesel,” Wright said during a discussion this week, according to Politico.
“We’re the largest diesel exporter in the world, but that same refinery that produces diesel also produces gasoline and jet fuel,” he continued. “So, if you can’t export the diesel that comes out of our refineries when you run out of places to store it, and you have to reduce U.S. refining, which would put upward pressure on gasoline prices and jet fuel prices.”
After being informed of the plan by Wright on Tuesday, energy CEOs quickly telephoned the White House to push back against the ban, an administration energy adviser told the outlet, adding: “It’s a terrible idea.”
One reported concern is that the 90-day ban could be extended. Another is that it could create a precedent for further government intervention in the private sector down the line.
An industry official told Politico that the fate of the proposal may come down to whoever is “the last person in the room” with the president.
Despite widespread opposition, the proposal may end up going into effect on account of political pressures the president is facing ahead of the midterm elections, now just six weeks away.
While Trump has long insisted higher fuel costs are a “small price to pay” for neutralizing Iran, most Americans don’t feel that way. Sixty-one percent of voters view prices at the pump as a significant concern, according to a September Fox News poll. And a number of GOP lawmakers have recently expressed that something must be done.
“What has overpowered cooler heads [in the White House] is the absolutely, sky-is-falling, we-have-to-do-something concern about prices at the pump” contingent, an oil industry executive told Politico. “That camp has been swept aside by the political camp, which says, ‘dammit, something has to happen.’”
The 80-year-old president is disposed to believe any backlash to the 90-day ban could be thought of as “a December problem,” the source said.
“This is not true,” a White House spokesperson told The Independent. “Politico published this Fake News even though the Energy Secretary publicly addressed this earlier today.”
The spokesperson pointed to comments from Wright delivered at the United Nations General Assembly, where he said the administration would not fully ban diesel exports, but instead implement restrictions.

articles.title_orig: Judge hears arguments on Trump White House media ban, hopes to rule 'soon'
articles.title_zh: Judge hears arguments on Trump White House media ban, hopes to rule 'soon'
articles.content_orig:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., heard arguments on Wednesday on President Donald Trump's controversial ban of three media outlets from the White House.
Judge Timothy Kelly ended the hearing without immediately ruling on a request by the outlets — MS NOW, CNN, Politico — to block Trump from continuing to bar them from the White House.
"I'll consider what you told me today. I'll try and get you an answer as soon as I can," Kelly told a lawyer for the outlets and a Justice Department attorney who defended the ban during the teleconference hearing that lasted about 46 minutes.
The outlets, in a lawsuit against Trump, argue the ban violates the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which protects free press rights by punishing them for the content of stories they have published about Trump and his administration.
"This is a clear retaliation case," Theodore Boutrous Jr., a lawyer representing the outlets, argued at Wednesday's hearing to Kelly, whom Trump nominated for his seat in U.S. District Court in D.C. in 2018.
The Justice Department, in a late Tuesday night filing, said Trump had barred the outlets on the grounds of national security concerns, and that the president had the legal right to do so. Trump did not cite that rationale when he announced the ban last Friday.
Kelly, at the beginning of the hearing, noted a 1977 ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit had found that media outlets were entitled to due process in any decision affecting an outlet's holding of so-called hard passes to the White House.
The three media outlets were not warned before Trump's announcement that he was considering yanking their hard pass access.
"I think it is fair to say that process ... wasn't followed here, talking about predeprivation process," Kelly said.
The judge noted that the Justice Department, in defending Trump's ban, argued that the 1977 ruling was wrong.
"There wasn't a semblance of due process here," said Boutrous. "This came completely out of the blue."
The attorney said Trump's public statements about the ban back up the outlets' argument that they are being targeted with "viewpoint discrimination" over how they cover the president and his administration.
Boutrous said that in Truth Social posts and in the Oval Office, Trump has said that he implemented the ban because "the coverage is too negative" and "purposely negative."
"He keeps saying the same thing," Boutrous said. "He keeps proving our point. He's literally our lead witness here."
Addressing the Justice Department's argument that the ban is justified on national security grounds, Boutrous said, "They're literally arguing that reporters shouldn't scrutinize national security."
The First Amendment protects the media's right to cover that subject, because "journalists can and should hold the government accountable," the attorney said.
Michael Velchik, an attorney for the Justice Department, opened his argument to Kelly by saying, "Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right."
Velchik also said, "The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security."
The attorney also said Trump was not acting in retaliation against the three outlets.
"The president criticizes many people," but has only applied the determination that led to his ban to the three outlets, Velchik said.
The attorney noted that Trump has called ABC News "the worst." But the president did not ban ABC from the White House.
The Justice Department, in its court filing Tuesday, appeared to react to the outlets' claim that they had been denied due process by including three separate letters to the outlets that cited the grounds for their purported "initial" banning, and giving them until this Friday to respond to avoid a permanent ban.
Kelly could issue his ruling at any time.
Kelly in 2018 ruled against the White House when he ordered that it restore the access pass of then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, who had it revoked after a contentious exchange with Trump.
Trump in announcing the ban Friday, accused the outlets of "cumulative" stories that contained so-called "fake news" about him and his administration.
The ban took effect on Saturday, with journalists from the outlets having their access passes taken away by the Secret Service when they arrived at the White House.
The three outlets jointly sued Trump on Monday.

articles.content_orig:
More than 80 tons of raw meat recalled as 'unsafe to eat'. See list
More than 160,000 pounds of raw meat sold nationwide has been recalled for being "unsafe to eat," according to a Sept. 22 notice from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS).
The more than 80 tons of raw pork, beef and goat were packaged and sold with fake USDA labels, according to FSIS, and were not actually properly inspected by the agency. As a result, the 167,639 pounds of recalled meat could be contaminated or contain undisclosed ingredients or allergens.
Star Meat Delivery Inc. initiated the recall after standard FSIS surveillance uncovered the false labels. While Star Meat produced the products, they were distributed by A&D Foods.
Federal officials are concerned the meat could be in the refrigerators or freezers of homes, restaurants or retailers. Here's what to know.
Which meat products were recalled?
All recalled products were sold at various weights in cardboard boxes containing individually vacuum-packed meats. They all have a fake USDA inspection label with the establishment number “EST. 1363."
The meat was shipped in bulk. It may have been repackaged with different labels after reaching stores. They were distributed nationwide by A&D Foods.

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years on Wednesday after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment.
Haley appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement.
In her statement, Haley spoke about the harassment and humiliation she has endured over the past seven years, saying she was publicly smeared by Weinstein, his defense team, and podcasters she suspects were paid to damage her image.
Haley added that her experience following the assault has “already been a life sentence” for her, and asked the judge to take all of this into consideration.
New York assistant district attorney Nicole Blumberg addressed the court on behalf of the prosecution. She asked the court to sentence Weinstein, 74, to 20 years with five years of post-release supervision, stating he never showed any type of remorse for his crimes.
Weinstein said in his statement he has remorse for Haley. “I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize for my actions,” he said.
Weinstein’s defense had also argued that their client is too sick to serve a long sentence following a diagnosis of several health conditions including blood cancer and heart disease. The defense asked for a nine-year sentence.
Before sentencing, Judge Curtis Farber acknowledged that Weinstein would be remembered not just for producing films, but for being the face of the #MeToo movement. Farber said Weinstein took advantage of Haley’s dreams of working in the film industry.
“You had it all,” Farber said. “Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley.”
The latest sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in the closely watched case.
Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in prison in 2020 after a jury convicted him of sexually assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actor Jessica Mann.
But in 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the convictions, saying Weinstein’s trial had been prejudiced by the judge allowing woman who alleged they were sexual assault victims of Weinstein to testify, despite not being plaintiffs in the case.
Weinstein went on trial again in 2025 and was once more convicted of a criminal sexual act involving Haley.
Jurors acquitted Weinstein of a separate sexual assault charge involving former model Kaja Sokola but could not reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann. Prosecutors retried the Mann charge earlier this year, but the jury deadlocked in May. The charge was later dropped after Mann said she could not endure another trial.
Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate California rape case.
In June, a California appeals court upheld Weinstein’s 2022 rape and sexual assault conviction. He was found guilty of assaulting an Italian model in her hotel room during a film festival.
He could serve the California sentence before beginning the sentence imposed in New York. Farber said at Wednesday’s sentencing that California will have the final say on whether Weinstein’s sentences run consecutively or concurrently.
The accusations and subsequent charges against Weinstein were one of the biggest factors in launching the #MeToo movement. More than 80 women have come forward with allegations of sexual assault or misconduct against him.

articles.title_orig: Tensions Rise Between Mamdani and Netanyahu as Israeli Leader Visits New York
articles.title_zh: Tensions Rise Between Mamdani and Netanyahu as Israeli Leader Visits New York
articles.content_orig:
The months-in-the-making clash between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Benjamin Netanyahu will come to a head on Thursday when the Israeli prime minister delivers a speech before the U.N. General Assembly in Manhattan.
The two are poised to become the focal point of the annual gathering of the world’s most powerful people, which brings motorcades, gridlock and demonstrations to the city. This year’s event comes with an additional layer of drama: During his mayoral campaign last year, Mamdani threatened to arrest Netanyahu on an International Criminal Court warrant. The mayor later clarified he doesn’t have the authority to arrest the prime minister, but has still called him a “war criminal.”
In a CNN interview released on Tuesday, Mamdani maintained his criticism, saying the warrant against Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity is “something that should be honored, because what we want to see, and we’ve been talking about this today, is a faith in our politics, a faith in accountability.”
Netanyahu teased his upcoming remarks on Tuesday with a video where he falsely accused the mayor of supporting Hamas and inciting riots against Jewish New Yorkers. He also delivered a direct message to Mamdani. “I'm coming to the U.N.,” he said. “I'm going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers and I'm going to tell the truth about you.”
Asked about the video, the mayor called Netanyahu the “architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians” and referenced ongoing Israeli attacks in Gaza.
The NYPD has warned protests are anticipated near the U.N. on Manhattan's East Side throughout the General Assembly. Mamdani has said he won’t attend protests against Netanyahu — noting he would uphold the right to demonstrate peacefully.
Sal Albanese, a former city councilmember who advised Mamdani on public safety, said he believed the mayor could balance the two interests of politics and public safety. Mamdani’s pro-Palestinian activism is a key part of his identity that fueled his election and continued popularity, he said. Similarly, protests are a fixture of the city.
“Netanyahu is obviously going to drive a lot of people on the street to protest,” he said. “As long as they do it peacefully, I don’t think it will be a problem.”
In July, Jewish leaders criticized the mayor for inflaming tensions with his criticism of Israel following the stabbings of a Jewish man and an Asian man on the Upper West Side. The attack occurred days after Mamdani had released a video acknowledging that he did not have the legal authority to order Netanyahu’s arrest. Nevertheless, he said Netanyahu was a “war criminal.”
This is not the first time a New York City mayor has clashed with a foreign leader in town for the General Assembly. In 1995, Mayor Rudy Giuliani directed his Chief of Staff Randy Mastro to ask Yasir Arafat, then the chair of the Palestine Liberation Organization, to leave a Lincoln Center concert. The Clinton administration issued a statement criticizing Giuliani’s actions.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
articles.content_orig:
Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, saying Iranians are "the victims of terrorism" by the U.S. and Israel, and have "never ever been an aggressor."
- A commercial vessel was struck in an attack in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, killing one crew member and necessitating the evacuation of more than 20 more sailors, according to the Omani navy.
- The Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened Wednesday to attack U.S. interests in the Middle East and to "close Bab el-Mandeb completely to American ships" if Washington joins Saudi-led military operations against the group in Yemen.
White House responds to Iranian president's speech at U.N.
President Trump is "courageously" fighting against the Iranian regime, the White House said Tuesday in response to a question about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's speech at the U.N. General Assembly.
"The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Anna Kelly, White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement. "The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable."
Through a translator, Pezeshkian said Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."
Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian said.
Canada imposes new sanctions on Iran officials, entities
The Canadian government announced new sanctions Wednesday against several senior Iranian officials and state-run entities "for their role in the Iranian regime's brutal repression of its population."
The sanctions target five senior Iranian security and government officials and five state-run entities, the foreign ministry said in a statement, without providing specifics.
"These individuals and entities have contributed to Iran's efforts to suppress dissent and restrict fundamental freedoms of Iran's population, including through digital surveillance, censorship, unlawful violence, arbitrary detention and intimidation," the ministry said.
A protest movement in Iran sparked in late December by grievances over high living costs rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on Jan. 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths from the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Rights groups based abroad put the toll higher and accused security forces of firing at demonstrators.
Massive protests also erupted in Iran in Sep. 2022 following the death in custody of Iranian Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested for allegedly violating strict dress rules for women.
UAE sanctions local branches of Iran's Bank Melli
The UAE central bank said Wednesday that it had imposed sanctions on the Emirati branches of Iran's Bank Melli, accusing it of violating local laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.
The bank said in a statement that "it has been decided to prohibit all branches of Bank Melli Iran operating in the UAE from conducting any financial transactions to and from Iran, including trade finance and fund transfers."
It cited "non-compliance with the regulations, laws and supervisory decisions in force in the UAE, including the requirements and obligations set out under the legislation related to combating money laundering, the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing."
The announcement comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, as well as Washington's more recent economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic.
As part of that stepped-up campaign, the U.S. announced new measures at the end of August targeting Iran's trading partners, and sanctioned the director of the Dubai branch of Bank Melli.
Last month, the United Arab Emirates announced the suspension of trade and financial exchanges with Tehran.
German foreign minister: "Iran must engage constructively" in negotiations
Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, offered a direct criticism of Iranian negotiations in a meeting with his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Iran must engage constructively in talks for a sustainable solution to end the conflict in the region & unconditionally open the Strait of Hormuz, ensuring free, safe and toll-free navigation for all," he said on social media.
Wadephul's comments came as Iran continues to take a hard line in negotiations, demanding the U.S. remove its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, end the war on all fronts, release frozen or restricted assets and agree to the Oman-Iran negotiated passage through the strait, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei.
Araghchi has yet to comment on the meeting with Wadephul, though the government shared photo of the two meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
Tehran reviewing U.S. response to its proposal, senior Iranian official tells Reuters
Iran is reviewing a U.S. response to its plan to end the fighting between the two countries, a senior Iranian official told the Reuters news agency on Wednesday, adding that many differences remain between the two sides.
The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the ending of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels were subjects discussed during indirect talks with the U.S. on Tuesday, the official said.
Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei said Wednesday in a long interview aired by state television network IRIB that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the U.S. met Iran's long-stated conditions.
"There is no staging or step-by-step process," he said. "Iran is trying to have this implemented within three or four days, within four or five days, for example."
"The next step will also be determined and specified by the Islamic Republic of Iran," Rezaei said.
Iran has long demanded the U.S. lift its blockade and return to the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding signed in June by President Trump and his Iranian counterpart, which Tehran quickly accused the U.S. of breaching by keeping the blockade in place.
1 dead, 27 evacuated from vessel struck in Strait of Hormuz, Oman navy says
One crew member is dead and 27 others have been evacuated after a commercial vessel was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman's royal navy said on social media, accompanied by a photo of the burning ship.
The crew member who was killed was a native of India, according to that country's Ministry of External Affairs. Twenty of the people on board the ship were Indian nationals, the agency said.
Oman identified the ship as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged merchant vessel Cape Dao.
The strike on a cargo vessel was reported earlier in the day by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center. The attack happened at about 7:30 a.m. local time.
The report from the UKMTO noted the ship was on fire and adrift, with Oman saying the ship was in the area of 2.5 nautical miles off the coast of the governorate of Musandam, which would correlate with the southern, U.S.-directed route through the Strait of Hormuz.
