articles.title_orig: As Xi Visits Washington, Trump Plays Down China’s Actions Against U.S. Interests
articles.title_zh: As Xi Visits Washington, Trump Plays Down China’s Actions Against U.S. Interests
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has spent years trying to squeeze China — imposing tariffs, cutting off access to advanced technology and pressing U.S. allies to reduce their dependence on Beijing. When he begins meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, he'll juxtapose the long-standing bluster with the pomp and circumstance the leaders lavish on each other.
And the two-day tête-à-tête will take place as Trump confronts a China that has proved harder to isolate and allies increasingly reluctant to line up behind the U.S. to do it.
Part of that is Beijing's doing. China has deepened trade ties around the world while building leverage of its own, most notably through rare earths. Its global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year, reaching a record $1.2 trillion for 2025 even as its exports to the U.S. dropped.
But the shift also reflects Trump's approach. Since returning to office, fights over tariffs, defense spending and personal spats have strained relationships with traditional allies even as Trump has pursued a more transactional relationship with Xi.
Countries Washington has traditionally counted on to magnify its power are increasingly seeking room to maneuver between the world's two largest economies.
As a result, Trump enters Thursday's summit facing a test of whether strains with U.S. allies have made it harder to marshal American power against Xi.
"China is presenting itself to the world as the stable counterweight to an erratic and violent United States," said Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution think tank. "America retains unmatched power on the world stage, but leverage requires a united front and there are a shrinking number of countries willing to follow America's lead right now."
For decades, one of the U.S.'s biggest advantages over China has been its network of allies and partners. When the U.S. restricted technology or imposed sanctions, bringing major economies in Europe and Asia along made those measures harder for Beijing to evade.
China still lacks anything comparable: The Lowy Institute, an independent Australian foreign-policy think tank, scored the U.S. defense networks at 81.4 on a scale of 100, versus 18.9 for China in 2025. But Beijing does not need U.S. allies to switch sides to erode that advantage. It only needs them to become less willing to move with Washington, Hass and other China experts said.
"When democratic countries don't have public support for a counterpart, it raises the cost for leaders to align with the United States," Hass told CNBC. "It lowers the cost for leaders to defy the United States."
Trump has taken a sledgehammer to relationships with allies. He's clashed with NATO over defense spending, threatened to reduce the U.S. troop presence in much of Europe while announcing plans Tuesday to add troops in Greenland after threatening to take over the island and imposed tariffs on the U.S.'s northern neighbor Canada.
"Although our biggest economic complaints regarding China's economy are shared by many of our allies and partners, the current U.S. approach is to attack all of those countries ... instead of forming a common front," said Melanie Hart, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub.
Meanwhile, public confidence in the U.S. as a reliable partner has fallen. In Canada, the share of people who described the U.S. as a reliable partner fell from 83% in 2022 to 35% this year, according to Pew Research Center in June. In Germany, the share who said Washington considers other countries' interests when making foreign policy fell from 60% in 2023 to 23%.
Canada this month was invited to be the first "associate member" of the European Union as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government seeks deeper defense ties with Europe and less reliance on the U.S.
Foreign allies "worry that as soon as they make a deal with us, Washington will undercut them in some way that they will then regret," Hart told CNBC.
China has sought to capitalize on that opening, not necessarily by persuading countries to choose Beijing over Washington, but by making the choice less binary.
The country remains a U.S. security partner and a strategic competitor of China, with troops from both countries still deployed along their disputed Himalayan border. Yet Xi visited India this month for the first time in seven years as the two countries took what Tanvi Madan, a senior fellow at Brookings, called "baby steps" toward stabilizing relations.
Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion in 2025, according to Chinese data, and Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed to strengthen business and transport links despite unresolved security disputes.
"Uncertainty over Trump's approach to Beijing and strains in India's own relationship with the U.S. have given India another reason to keep relations with China on steadier ground," Madan told CNBC. "Even a tactical détente between the U.S., India and China can have downstream impacts on India's strategic environment."
The changing balance of leverage is most tangible in the economic relationship.
Trump's tariffs targeted China's reliance on U.S. buyers, while U.S. export controls targeted a deeper dependency: the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment Beijing needs to compete at the technological frontier.
Those pressure points remain. But Beijing has developed leverage of its own. China placed seven rare-earth elements under export controls last year, forcing companies to seek government approval to ship them abroad. China accounted for more than 70% of global rare-earth mining and more than 87% of refining and production in 2024, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
In short order, Ford halted Explorer production in Chicago for a week amid magnet shortages, while Japanese and European auto suppliers shut production lines awaiting materials.
Suddenly, the U.S. faced a version of the vulnerability it had spent years trying to create for Beijing: dependence on something the other side could withhold.
"One of China's primary objectives ahead of these meetings is to box the U.S. in diplomatically, to limit the Trump administration's range of action," Hart said, pointing to critical minerals as one tool Beijing has used.
That vulnerability now hangs over Thursday's summit. The current trade truce expires Nov. 10. Rare earths were again on the table in weekend talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Bessent said Wednesday after another meeting with He that the U.S. was "fine with either continuing" the current truce or "examining [a] bigger deal."
Meanwhile, Trump has other cards to play.
U.S. and allied firms control critical parts of the advanced semiconductor ecosystem, and American restrictions limit China's access to its most sophisticated chips and manufacturing equipment. Trump has also allowed limited sales of Nvidia's H200 AI chips to China even as broader restrictions remain in place, making semiconductor access another bargaining point.
That bargaining dynamic is beginning to reach beyond trade.
A $14 billion U.S. arms package for Taiwan has been awaiting Trump's approval for months. After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the package in abeyance and called it a "very good negotiating chip."
For Beijing, few issues carry higher stakes. China claims Taiwan as its sovereign territory and has never renounced the use of force to achieve unification. Xi also pressed Trump on U.S. arms sales and Taiwan during their May meeting.
The delayed arms deal has raised concern among U.S. allies in Asia that Trump could soften Washington's position on Taiwan in exchange for economic concessions from Xi.
But Hart said Beijing's objective goes beyond one arms package.
"Their bigger play will be getting him to feel like he has a deal with Xi Jinping underway" in which Trump believes he needs to hold back U.S. support for Taiwan

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.content_orig:
A court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men on terrorist charges for their involvement in the deadly 2019 Easter bombings and sentenced them each to at least 220 years in prison.
The terror attacks, which targeted luxury hotels and churches as they held Easter services, left 267 people dead and wounded almost 600. The bombings, which were inspired by Islamic State (IS), were among the deadliest terror attacks in Sri Lanka’s history and sent shockwaves through the country.
Two Sri Lanka-based Islamist militant groups were believed to have orchestrated the attacks. A video, recorded by the suicide bombers the day before the bombings, showed the attackers with their faces covered, armed with rifles and swords and pledging allegiance to the then-IS leader Abu Bakhr al-Baghdadi to make Sri Lanka an Islamic nation and wage war.
The attacks were carried out by nine suicide bombers who died in the blasts. None of those who directly participated survived.
Those on trial were accused of conspiring and aiding the bombings, which had deliberately targeted the minority Christian community and foreign tourists. The proceedings had spanned nearly five years, with the slow pace of justice frustrating victims and their families.
In 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 25 suspects whom they accused of planning or inspiring the attacks: three at churches, three at tourist hotels, one at a motel where an attacker killed himself, and two others after aborting a plan to attack a fourth hotel. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offences under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
The verdict was finally delivered on Tuesday by a three-judge high court amid tight security, with hundreds of police deployed around the courthouse.
In total, 15 defendants, who were all from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community, were sentenced to more than 200 years each. The judges also ordered the property of the defendants to be confiscated.
Nine defendants were freed after the court found that the charges against them were not proven. One other died before their case reached trial.
“Finally, we have justice,” said Catholic priest Jude Fernando. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.”
However, the completion of the trial is unlikely to offer full closure for some. Sri Lanka’s Catholic church has long alleged that perpetrators put on trial were not the masterminds behind the bombings.
Since Sri Lanka’s new government was elected in late 2024, there have been renewed investigations into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state – tied to former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa and his powerful family dynasty – may have had links to those responsible for the attacks.
Investigators have alleged the Easter bombings were part of a conspiracy to manufacture a security threat, that would create chaos and help bring Rajapaksa, a former defence chief, to power.
Rajapaksa was elected as president just a few months after the attack, on the back of a campaign that portrayed him as a strongman leader who was tough on terror.
A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks. In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence ministry official were sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.
Earlier this year, police also arrested Suresh Salley, a former intelligence chief and retired army major general, alleging he had prior knowledge of the attacks and worked with Islamist extremists before the bombings were carried out. He remains in custody but denies the charges.
The country’s defence ministry and the Rajapaksa family have denied any involvement in the attacks.

articles.title_orig: Modal Motors is trying to cut China out of electric motors entirely
articles.title_zh: Modal Motors is trying to cut China out of electric motors entirely
articles.content_orig:
Lately, it seems like everyone is talking about bringing manufacturing back to the United States, especially when it comes to hard tech like drones and robotics. Michael Van Steenburg thinks he’s ahead of the game.
Van Steenburg spent the last decade building all kinds of electric motors in the U.S. and North America, and now he wants to do it again with his new startup, Modal Motors. This time, he wants to ditch rare-earth magnets entirely, in a bid to further separate the U.S. from China’s supply chain.
As one of the founders in Startup Battlefield 200 who will compete at TechCrunch Disrupt next month, he thinks it’s an urgent pitch to make.
“China’s already flexed its muscles a couple times,” Van Steenburg said, referring to the country restricting access to rare-earth products.
There are other companies working on setting up electric motor manufacturing and supply chains in the U.S., but Van Steenburg argues they’re doing it the wrong way by continuing to rely on rare-earth magnets. Domestic supply of those materials is still years away, he said.
“Other people are ‘reshoring,’ [but] they’re basically knocking off Chinese motors and just doing it in the U.S. But they’re hoping that the U.S. rare-earth magnet system is going to get up to speed fast enough,” he said. “It’s going to still be a while longer before they can actually replace China.”
Modal Motors has two products that it’s developing ahead of Disrupt. One is a small electric motor meant for drones that can also work in fans, blowers, and even actuators. It’s designed to “minimize mass while delivering maximum torque density and efficiency,” according to the startup’s website.
The more radical design is what Modal refers to as the “Hybrid Enigma Drive,” a planar — or flat — electric motor that can fit in lower-profile spaces.
Van Steenburg is drawing on decades of experience in the automotive industry to develop these motors and get them customer-ready. But there’s also an irony in the work Van Steenburg is doing to make Modal Motors’ products a China-free option; in the late 1990s, he worked on a hybrid gas-electric drivetrain that China wanted to put in its so-called “People’s Car.”
“It’s kind of comical,” he said, thinking back on that experience and how much the world has changed. What hasn’t changed, he said, is his outsider streak and strong conviction about doing things that are hard.
“I always tell people that the clock started ticking 25 years ago, and in that whole time, I’ve watched a slow-motion train wreck as China’s been going around the world, grabbing mines, grabbing mineral rights, doing all these things, and slowly but surely monopolizing the entire rare-earth supply chain,” he said.

articles.title_orig: As Trump and Xi meet, Chinese automakers could be a Pandora's box for U.S. auto industry
articles.title_zh: As Trump and Xi meet, Chinese automakers could be a Pandora's box for U.S. auto industry
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — As President Donald Trump meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, U.S. politicians as well as the global automotive industry are warning that allowing Chinese automakers to enter the market could be a Pandora's box.
Trump earlier this month said he might be "OK" letting Chinese automakers into the U.S. if they produced vehicles domestically, leading a consortium of auto trade groups representing every major facet of the American auto industry to urge him to rethink that position.
It was an uncharacteristically unified message from automakers operating in the U.S., franchised dealers and suppliers. More than two dozen Democratic lawmakers followed that push with their own letter, urging Trump to keep in place U.S. restrictions against Chinese automakers.
"It's not at this point a partisan issue," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., told reporters Wednesday. "It's about whether we want to make cars in America and whether we want a manufacturing base that can pivot when we need it. If we want that, we shouldn't let them in our country."
Trump is scheduled to host Xi and a delegation from China on Thursday and Friday that reportedly could include Wang Chuanfu, founder of BYD, China's largest automaker, and Robin Zeng, founder of CATL, the world's top battery maker for electric vehicles.
Michael Dunne, an expert on China's automotive industry and a former General Motors executive, said even the potential that those two executives could attend underscores the importance of Xi's trip for the U.S. auto industry.
GM CEO Mary Barra is also expected to be among the attendees at Trump's state dinner for Xi, Reuters reported Wednesday, along with several other U.S. executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
As for America's other largest automakers, Ford Motor declined to disclose whether CEO Jim Farley will be attending after the Department of Transportation criticized the company for its Chinese ties, including a licensing deal with CATL. Reuters reported Chrysler parent Stellantis said CEO Antonio Filosa is out of the country and not planning to attend.
Industry insiders and onlookers have expressed concerns similar to those raised by automakers and lawmakers as bipartisan bills to ban Chinese automakers from the U.S. move through Congress.
The pressure campaign comes as Chinese automakers have been rapidly expanding outside of their domestic market, especially to Europe and Central and South America. There's fear among global automakers that Chinese rivals, like BYD and Geely, which are heavily subsidized by their governments, could flood global markets, undercutting domestic production and vehicle prices.
Dunne said he doesn't believe those concerns are overblown. He said Chinese automakers would "quickly overwhelm America's auto industry, just as it is now ravaging Europe."
Global market share for Chinese brands jumped nearly 70% from 2020 to 2025, according to market research and consulting firm GlobalData. The automakers' market share in Europe was virtually nothing in 2020 but hit 12% in August, according to Germany-based Dataforce.
"China's scores of automakers are currently engaged in a fight-to-the-death price war at home," Dunne wrote in a post Monday. "There's red ink everywhere. Access to the U.S., by far the most lucrative car market in the world, is like a giant tank of life-saving oxygen."
'Attacking very aggressively'
For much of this century, China was one of the largest and fastest-growing markets in the world. Non-China automakers flocked to the historically enclosed country with hopes of massive sales and profits.
But after years of success for automakers such as GM, the Chinese automotive sector has rapidly changed from an insular industry to the biggest exporter of vehicles globally.
China's growth has been fueled by government funding for companies as well as a culture of innovation and speed the country has instilled in its workers, experts said. The decision to ramp up exports has come on the heels of a slowing Chinese market and plant underutilization.
Christian Meunier, Nissan Motor chairman of the Americas, described competing against Chinese automakers as a "hell of a challenge" in countries outside of the U.S.
"They have decent product but it's all dumping," he told CNBC during a recent interview. "We know we're not competing with [automakers], we're competing against the governments. … They're attacking very aggressively."
Meunier said the Japanese automaker has been trying to battle the Chinese as best as it can through growing scale globally to lower costs and become more efficient.
"We need to get ready for the day when they come to the U.S. because it will happen one day. Hopefully not tomorrow, but it will happen one day," he said.
Dunne said China's ambitions and ways of doing business are vastly different from those of U.S. allies, which makes it different from allowing imports from Japan, South Korea and other countries.
"As Xi Jinping has alluded to many times, the goal for China is to 'make other countries more dependent on China and China less dependent on other countries.' That's not a friendly posture," Dunne said.
— CNBC's Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
articles.title_zh: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
articles.content_orig:
Kremlin yet to respond publicly to US invitation that is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and EU countries
The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York.
“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”
The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies.
Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club.
Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”.
The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries.
European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit.
Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended.
“We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.”
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy addressed the United Nations, urging world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war effort.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelenskyy. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.”
Zelenskyy also warned that the war could spread beyond Ukraine if Putin was not stopped.
Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”.
Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices.
In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress.
Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy.
“President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet.
For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens.
On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke.
A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station.
Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well.
In response to what has happened, the House foreign affairs committee posted on X : “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.”
Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv

articles.content_orig:
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko revealed during a speech to youth leaders in Minsk that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin regularly joke and argue over which of them qualifies as the ultimate dictator.
The Belarusian leader's comments at "Youth. Belarus. Future." Sept. 17 also underlines the close alignment between Moscow and Minsk with Lukashenko enjoying his position as Europe’s longest-serving head of state.
Lukashenko has ruled over Belarus unhindered since 1994, with Putin leading Russia since 2012, also serving as president between 2000 and 2008.
"You know what they say about me?" Lukashenko asked the audience during his Sept. 17 address, according to Novaya Gazeta.
TRUMP SAYS US HELPED SECURE RELEASE OF 5 PRISONERS IN BELARUS DEAL, THANKS LUKASHENKO
"[I am] the last dictator, the second-to-last dictator in Europe. Dictator, dictator. Vladimir Putin and I often joke and argue over which of us is more of a dictator.
"They say I’m the last dictator, the last dictator in Europe. Dictator — so be it. Well, Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin and I often argue, jokingly, about which of us is the bigger dictator."
Lukashenko, 72, a former Soviet collective farm manager, is also known to be Putin’s closest international partner and ally.
While Minsk has not committed ground troops to the war in Ukraine, it serves as a strategic staging ground for Moscow, with Russia relying on Belarus for military and strategic support in its ongoing war against Ukraine.
According to the Kyiv Post, Belarus specifically provides Russia with key weapons components and allows its forces to launch military strikes from Belarusian territory.
An August report by Ukrainska Pravda also highlighted a new railway construction capable of handling military trains in Belarus' Gomel Oblast near the Ukraine border.
RUSSIA’S STRIKES NEAR MOLDOVA RAISE ALARM OVER PUTIN’S PLANS FOR EUROPE’S EASTERN FLANK
The strength of the relationship between the two countries comes as Western officials increase pressure on Moscow and its allies and with the two leaders reported to be in frequent contact.
After meeting in Moscow Aug. 27, Lukashenko officially congratulated Putin Sept. 21 after the Russian election results.
He praised the "unprecedented turnout of millions of voters" and the majority secured by the United Russia party, calling it a proper response to "cynical attempts from the outside to discredit the campaign and sow discord."
Addressing the youth forum in Minsk on political succession in Belarus, Lukashenko insisted no one is prepared to take over power.
"Never believe those who say that Lukashenko is ‘clinging to power with blue-knuckled hands’," he told the audience.
"Good Lord, let them say it. I have had my fill of this power to the point where I could not possibly want any more of it.
"The only question is whether you are capable today of taking over the country and holding on to it," he added. "If you are, start tomorrow. To be frank, I cannot yet answer that question positively. Do not take offense.
"I became a dictator then because I stood up against the entire ‘civilized world.'"
Western nations maintain strict economic pressure on Minsk. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys recently reiterated the Baltic nation's firm stance.
"We do not see any reasons why our position on Belarus should soften as Belarus is not changing its behavior," Budrys said.
"On our side, we have to be very exact and continue what works, and that is the pressure on the regime."
Despite international sanctions, Lukashenko announced Sept. 11 that Belarus has begun selling potash, a primary export used in fertilizer, to the United States.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Western nations maintain economic restrictions over human rights abuses, U.S. sanctions on Belarusian potash were lifted after recent political prisoner releases, though European Union sanctions remain active.

articles.title_orig: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose of drugs, including fentanyl, coroner says
articles.title_zh: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose of drugs, including fentanyl, coroner says
articles.content_orig:
“Heroes” and “Nashville” star Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled an accident caused by the toxic effects of multiple drugs, including fentanyl, officials said Tuesday.
The Greenville County Coroner’s Office attributed her cause of death to the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol and Quetiapine.
There were no signs of trauma that would have contributed to the death, the release added.
Panettiere, 36, died Aug. 16 at a South Carolina apartment complex where she had been staying. Authorities found her unresponsive after a report of a cardiac arrest.
She had been in rehab just weeks before, according to a coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press.
The detailed report released to the AP said a senior deputy coroner investigating the death discovered blue pressed pills and a straw on a table at the Airbnb apartment where the actor had been staying. It tested positive for fentanyl, according to the report, which also noted that a white powdery substance was found in her suitcase in a sunglasses case.
When the investigator called Panettiere’s father, he said she planned to spend her birthday five days later in Greenville, then head to Ukraine to visit her daughter.
In a statement Wednesday in response to the release of Panettiere’s cause of death, her mother, Lesley Vogel, called her daughter a “fighter.”
“She proudly owned this badge and I respected her prowess,” Vogel said. “She was transparent with her addictions and her numerous rehab attempts show her resolve to live a healthy life. We are all responsible for our choices.”
She added: “The loss of Hayden is palpable; grief permeates the soul and it will live with those who loved her forever. Let us not dishonor the amazing talent, intellect and beauty of this young woman who left this Earth far too soon.”
The Greenville Police Department said there were no signs of foul play during the initial response and investigation. The investigation into her death remains active, the department said Tuesday.
The Drug Enforcement Administration was also investigating Panettiere’s death.
Bill Bodner, the former special agent in charge of the DEA’s Los Angeles Field Division, noted that the quantity of drugs found in Panettiere’s system remains unclear. But three of the drugs listed in her autopsy became common among drug abusers in the 1990s and remain widely used.
The cocktail’s street name, he said, is “the Holy Trinity.”
Bodner identified those drugs as an opiate, which in Panettiere’s case was fentanyl; a muscle relaxer, or Methocarbamol; and an anti-anxiety medication, or Alprazolam.
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic drug typically used to treat conditions such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. 4-ANPP, or 4-Anilinopiperidine, is a precursor chemical used in the illicit manufacture of fentanyl, Bodner said.
He described the precursor as a likely sign that the fentanyl found in her system was illegal. The drug cocktail, he added, is “incredibly dangerous.”
“When used in combination, there’s a synergism,” he said.
Vogel said that despite Panettiere’s public struggles with addiction, she has “never heard Hayden speak of Fentanyl.” One exception, she said, was when Panettiere “warned her brother of the dangers as well as orchestrating his rehabilitation,” adding that her daughter “would never have chosen” the drug.
Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was at the apartment complex at the time of her death and showed authorities what a police report described as a “bag of medication” he said she was taking.
An attorney for Hickerson did not immediately respond Tuesday to a request for comment on Panettiere’s death.
Bodner, who probed the overdose deaths of Michael Jackson, Matthew Perry and other celebrities, has said investigators were likely attempting to reconstruct Panettiere’s final days.
“They will use forensics to exploit her telephone, try to re-create the last two or three days of her life from looking at text messages, looking at phone calls, looking at interaction with people on social media,” the 32-year veteran of the DEA’s field office in Los Angeles said.
“Once there’s a timeline of what she was doing before her death, it becomes easier to kind of find where that drug distribution took place that killed her,” Bodner added.
Panettiere’s relationship with Hickerson — an aspiring actor from South Carolina — appeared to have ended in 2020 amid allegations of domestic violence, but her mother told NBC News that they were still seeing each other when she died.
Panettiere detailed those allegations, along with her struggles with addiction and postpartum depression, in her recently released memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning.”
Hickerson pleaded no contest to a charge of injuring a spouse or girlfriend in 2019 in Los Angeles, and he was sentenced to four years of probation, court records show. Panettiere sought a restraining order against Hickerson in 2020, though the outcome is unclear.
In a statement in August, a lawyer for Hickerson reiterated that police found no signs of foul play in Panettiere’s death. The attorney, Sloan Ellis, added that the actor’s death remained under investigation.
“Out of respect for Hayden’s loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time,” Ellis said at the time.
Panettiere began appearing in television commercials as a child. She landed a breakout role on the NBC sci-fi series “Heroes” and later earned two Golden Globe nominations for portraying an ambitious and volatile country musician in “Nashville.”
In her memoir, Panettiere wrote that her life began to spiral after she had a daughter with Ukrainian heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She began drinking heavily to cope with postpartum depression and Klitschko’s distance, she wrote.
Panettiere checked into rehab and gave Klitschko custody of their child in 2018.
If you or someone you know is struggling with a drug or substance abuse problem, call these numbers for help: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s national helpline is 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357); the National Drug Helpline is 1-844-289-0879; and the American Addiction Centers’ hotline is (866) 464-3073.

articles.title_orig: China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents - International Consortium of Investigative Journalists
articles.title_zh: China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents - International Consortium of Investigative Journalists
articles.content_orig:
China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents
ICIJ’s media partners uncovered strategic deals and moves the Chinese bank made around the world to further the political priorities of the party-state.
China Capital, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists in collaboration with 23 media partners, provided an unprecedented look into decision-making at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, one of the most powerful Chinese institutions, at a time of China’s ascendance on the world stage.
The investigation is based on more than 4.8 million confidential records from two of ICBC’s U.K. units. The records provide rare insight into one of China’s most important financial arms, showing how the government’s influence and political priorities often outweigh ordinary banking protocols.
This is the first time that an international team of reporters has examined the inner workings and lending practices of ICBC– the world’s largest bank by asset size. Like many of its state-owned peers, ICBC is notoriously secretive.
“The ICIJ investigation shows how branch structures can be leveraged by foreign bank headquarters to override local compliance officers when state-backed corporate interests conflict with local regulatory obligations,” said David P. Weber, an accounting professor at West Virginia University and former Chief Investigator of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. He urged regulators in the U.S. and the U.K. to implement a cross-border enforcement mechanism that could “reduce oversight fragmentation.”
From New Zealand to Mexico, the 75 journalists who participated in the investigation uncovered previously unknown details about the bank’s involvement in some of their countries’ most important infrastructure projects and natural resources companies, as well as deals with firms linked to China’s military apparatus. Here are some of the revelations they uncovered.
The bank did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment.
How ICBC blended commercial interests with China’s political priorities
ICIJ’s partners across India, New Zealand and Austria found repeated instances where the bank’s political role blended with its commercial interests.
In 2017, Indian and Chinese troops reached a stand-off in the disputed Doklam region at the two countries’ borders, after the Indian government accused Beijing-backed companies of building roads in a territory claimed by China and Bhutan, in violation of a 1980 treaty. The two-month face-off didn’t just have political repercussions, The Indian Express, an ICIJ partner, reported. It also triggered actions inside ICBC’s Mumbai branch, more than 1,200 miles south of the border.
Soon after the news reached the bankers, ICBC “suspended the disbursement of 11 approved but undisbursed loans and bond investments totalling $185 million,” according to internal records. The bank also “organized” Chinese Communist Party members across every department to stay in constant touch with China’s embassy and consulate. The incident exemplifies the bank’s tight links to the party-state and how geopolitical events can influence its lending operations around the world.
Like most Chinese companies, ICBC has a Communist Party committee, an internal cell that ensures its operations advance the party’s interests, and some bankers were internally referred to as “comrades.”
In New Zealand, The Post reported that a Communist Party member who worked as a senior executive at ICBC’s Auckland outpost handled the local accounts of Hikvision, a Chinese surveillance tech company with links to the government. Numerous investigations by researchers and journalists have documented how, since at least 2017, Hikvision has provided surveillance technology to forces in Xinjiang, the Chinese region where Xi Jinping’s government has waged a repression campaign against hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities. In 2020, the U.S. government blacklisted the firm for enabling human rights abuses.
Internal ICBC records describe how Lu Ping, the chief marketing officer of the ICBC subsidiary in New Zealand, “exhibited the outstanding qualities of a communist party member.” “Comrade Lu Ping” was nominated for a company-wide commendation in 2022 for his proactive role “fulfilling cash management needs” in New Zealand for Hikvision and Huawei, one of the bank’s most important clients.
China Capital also uncovered secret links between one of Austria’s most important aviation companies and a top Chinese producer of military aircraft. ICIJ’s partner in Vienna, profil, examined internal 2021 memos that discussed a $230 million loan to Future Advance Composite Components, which is affiliated with the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China.
While FACC, as the firm is known, publicly states that it produces aircraft parts exclusively for the civilian market, its Chinese owner has an “absolute leading position” in China’s defense industry and is the “sole manufacturer of all kinds of military aircraft and airborne equipment” in the country, according to the records.
ICBC bankers also discussed the possibility that the U.S. government could sanction AVIC in the future due to its links to China’s military apparatus. Though some London officers opposed extending the loans due to risk management concerns, they left the ultimate decision to ICBC’s Beijing headquarters. The documents do not state whether the bank approved the loan. AVIC did not respond to inquiries from profil.
Strategic deals revealed across Australia, Ghana, Belgium, the UK and Sweden
As part of China Capital, reporters also examined hundreds of credit application forms and other records that partly explained why ICBC London would want to pursue a deal. The documents revealed the geopolitical nature of some loans.
In Australia, ICBC issued “loss-making or marginal loans” to some of the country’s biggest resources and infrastructure companies, including Rio Tinto, Fortescue and Glencore, as a way of starting long-term relationships that would help advance Beijing’s political goals, the Australian Financial Review found.
The documents show how in 2015, Andrew Forrest, the billionaire CEO of Fortescue, an iron ore miner, made an emergency trip to Beijing to meet with ICBC’s chairman and seek assistance after the company was forced to cancel a $2.5 billion bond issuance because of unattractive interest rates.
Fortescue was struggling financially, but ICBC’s Sydney branch implored the Beijing headquarters to approve the loan at rates close to 30% below those offered by bond investors in the U.S., AFR reported. An internal memo cited Fortescue’s “significant strategic importance for the Chinese steel industry.”
ICIJ media partners in Ghana found evidence of loans awarded for similarly strategic reasons.
Ghana Business News reported how ICBC continued to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to the Ghana Cocoa Board, a government entity that supports and controls the production of cocoa — an important commodity — even though the company lacked transparency and was on a watchlist of borrowers in financial distress.
According to internal records, China stood to benefit from financing the firm, also known as Cocobod, since Chinese trade companies were key buyers and the deal helped cement the political alliance between Beijing and Accra. ICBC’s Brussels branch also participated in the loan to Cocobod, De Tijd reported, suggesting that the overseas units often helped each other when the clients were considered strategic for the bank and the party-state.
ICBC acquired a key role in the China-Africa trade thanks to its 19.7% stake in South African banking giant Standard Bank, The Africa Report found. Chinese authorities have approved the two institutions as joint renminbi-clearing banks — an arrangement that is expected to ease transactions in the Chinese currency across 19 countries where Standard Bank

articles.title_orig: What China’s Vibe-Coding Capital Can Tell Us About the A.I. Boom
articles.title_zh: What China’s Vibe-Coding Capital Can Tell Us About the A.I. Boom
articles.content_orig:
In mid-May, days after Donald Trump visited Beijing, a Chinese tech founder named Levy invited me to an office party for his A.I. fortune-telling company. It’s called FateTell, and it makes an app that, in the vein of traditional Chinese astrology, reads your bazi, a chart that tracks the elemental forces associated with your birth date and time. (Levy wanted me at the event because of the makeup of my bazi. According to his invitation, my governing element, fire, would counteract the water element that Levy carries in oversupply.) So I travelled from Beijing to FateTell’s headquarters, situated on the edge of Hangzhou—one of China’s tech hubs, home to Alibaba and the insurgent Chinese A.I. company DeepSeek—in a town called Liangzhu.
Liangzhu means “beautiful waterland,” and it more than earns the name—rivers, lakes, and marshes thread through the low hills at the town’s edge. The town is hip, idyllic, contrarian, and increasingly known as an escape for workers burnt out by the grind of China’s booming tech industry. To those back in Beijing or Shenzhen, Liangzhu has become a low-cost retreat where people can afford to vibe-code—building software through conversations with A.I., as opposed to writing source code at a line-by-line level–on their own terms, without having to work what is known as the 9-9-6, an extreme schedule that is common in Chinese tech firms of working from 9 A.M. to 9 P.M., six days a week.
Residents often dub themselves “villagers,” and describe Liangzhu as between rural and suburban. Between verdant parks and wide avenues, they sit on sprawling grass fields—a way of relaxing that is rare in most major Chinese cities, where lawns are usually cordoned off. Often, there is a stroller parked next to them. (China’s birth rate has plummeted to its lowest point since 1949, but, in the area where Liangzhu is, the birth rate is double the national average).
It didn’t take me long after my arrival in Liangzhu to stumble upon the town’s growing population of vibe-coders. Near Liangzhu’s cultural and art center, a sprawling structure designed by Tadao Ando and surrounded by cherry blossoms, I overheard young developers murmuring about Kimi, a Chinese large language model, and OpenAI’s Codex. Some had dogs at their feet. Others were coding over oat-milk lattes. The building’s nickname, I learned, is the Big Roof. Nearby stands another towering structure, called the Big Barn, which contains a vast bookstore. The structures, made of raw concrete, exuded an ostentatious form of modesty, emblematic of the town’s character.
Everywhere I went, people were building new A.I. products. This is not unique to Liangzhu. In the past few years, as the A.I. boom went global, Beijing has made A.I. a national priority, launching a campaign known as A.I. Plus to seed it throughout the economy. China’s major tech companies are bracing for the same transformation, pouring money into semiconductors, large language models, and cloud infrastructure, as well as the consumer products that are built on top of them. But, unlike the everything apps that are favored by most of these big tech companies, much of the software built in Liangzhu is whimsical and quirky, similar in spirit to an artisanal craft you might pick up at a small-scale farmers’ market. FocusFlight, a timer that simulates an immersive flight environment to improve concentration, plays white noise while you “fly” to a city. (As I wrote this piece, I “flew” from San Francisco to Los Angeles.) YouMind, an A.I. workflow tool, bills itself as a “second brain” that helps people “create bolder” by gathering scattered reading, notes, and research in one place and turning it into finished work (one of their ads is an A.I.-generated video that tells the story of an exhausted mother with no income, trying to write as a baby cries in the background; later, she is pictured using YouMind, and becomes happy and successful). And then there is FateTell, which feeds your bazi through large language models and spits out guides “based on thousands of years of Eastern wisdom.” The app has hundreds of thousands of users, the most devoted of whom pay an annual fee to subscribe. (Levy told me they’re also exploring a hardware direction: making wooden blocks shaped like moons—traditional divination tools that are thrown to seek spiritual guidance—embedded with smart chips.)
In fact, a throwback to traditional Chinese spirituality and Western New Age practices pervades much of the town. I checked a local event guide during my visit; it included an I Ching guide to dressing for luck, a Zen sutra reading, and an essential-oils workshop for healing. A singing-bowl sound-therapy studio sat beside a boutique that sold only linen and silk clothing, cut loose and draping enough to make the wearer look faintly monk-like. Crystals were in one shop window; tarot upstairs. Astrology, consumerism, and A.I. were folded into one another as though they had always belonged together—reminiscent of an older era of Silicon Valley when spirituality and personal computing grew out of the same countercultural milieu. I asked Ian Johnson, a Canadian-American reporter who won a Pulitzer Prize for his coverage of Chinese religious life in the early two-thousands, about the way spirituality was manifesting among young people in the A.I. generation. “They’re like the Woodstock generation in the West,” he told me. Johnson explained that the previous generation in China underwent rapid economic development and huge leaps in the availability of material goods. For their children, existential questions have emerged, and in the fast-moving, chaotic tech world, he added, uncertainty feels especially acute. “Why one company succeeds and another fails can seem almost metaphysical,” Johnson said.
Levy, the founder of FateTell, is a star in Liangzhu. A graduate of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, he once worked at ByteDance, the company that created TikTok. He is lean, with a slight frame and a calculating gaze—though he speaks softly and contemplatively. He told me he has long been interested in how technology intersects with spirituality, referencing both the I Ching and Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” and, after I told him that I live in the Bay Area, he said, with a small conspiratorial grin, that he had cast the bazi of every major A.I. leader. His reading of Sam Altman’s bazi: “a mercenary accountant.” Elon Musk, he said, “will have a very bumpy few years.” He had almost named the company Muad’Dib, after the nickname that the character Paul Atreides takes among the Fremen in “Dune,” but FateTell had the benefit of being slightly more literal.
At the party, Levy introduced me to the FateTell team, a group of eight people, among whom almost no moment goes un-astrologized. One engineer took a two-week vow of silence because his bazi had warned him that he was losing his sense of self by excessively describing his life—an increasingly common affliction for a generation immersed in Chinese social media. All eight employees had had their charts checked for compatibility before being hired. The C.O.O. treated my bazi as if it were as important as my last name and warned me, “The Year of the Fire Horse might bring you fame, but also exhaustion and illness.”
Before entering the tech world, Levy had considered becoming a Taoist monk. “Years ago, a great master told me I had a gift for the spirit,” he said. “He nearly took me up into the mountains to cultivate the Tao.” But Levy’s love of A.I. proved the stronger pull, and he instead attempted to merge Taoism with that. “I’ve wanted to build a Taoist app since 2017,” he explained. “The years since have been preparation—I met hundreds of practitioners and diviners, and read my way through the classical scriptures.” Then, after DeepSeek launched, he was convinced that the time had finally come.
It was late 2024, a year after Xi Jinping had named A.I. an essential engine for China’s “new quality productive

articles.title_orig: Mamdani roasted for staying tight-lipped on 'war criminal' Pezeshkian after raging about Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Mamdani roasted for staying tight-lipped on 'war criminal' Pezeshkian after raging about Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Fox News correspondent Alexis McAdams reports on New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of his visit to the United Nations. Israeli Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon joins 'America Reports' to react to the controversial comments and discuss the threat of Iran-backed attacks against regional allies.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani repeatedly branded Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal," but faced criticism for remaining largely tight-lipped about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
While Mamdani has labeled the Iranian government "brutal" and cited its "systematic repression of its own people," critics railed against him for declining to use similar language about Pezeshkian, who arrived in the city on Wednesday.
"Mayor Mamdani, you said war criminals who set foot in New York should be arrested. Good news. One is in New York city this week," said Iranian-born journalist Masih Alinejad, who was subjected to an assassination attempt near her Brooklyn home while Ayatollah Ali Hosseini Khamenei was still alive.
"If you have the courage to talk about arresting those responsible for crimes against humanity, start with the man sleeping five miles from your office," Alinejad tweeted .
TRUMP, IRANIAN PRESIDENT CONVERGE ON NYC FOR ‘DRAMATIC’ UN SHOWDOWN AS TEHRAN FACES TIGHT RESTRICTIONS
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani branded Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal" and urged the federal government to arrest him under an International Criminal Court warrant on July 21, 2026. ((L) Reuters, (R) @NYCMayor via X)
She invited Mamdani to view the FBI files about her case, in which several men attempted to kidnap her in Brooklyn.
Director of National Intelligence Walter "Jay" Clayton said in January that the Iranian regime coordinated a murder-for-hire plot against Alinejad because of her efforts to speak out against its human rights abuses, while federal authorities sentenced one U.S.-based conspirator to 15 years.
"The government of Iran, a sponsor of terrorism, assassination, and espionage around the globe, has engaged in a campaign of assassination plots in the United States and abroad targeting those who oppose the regime," Clayton said in a statement.
MAMDANI MAKES EYEBROW-RAISING CLAIM ABOUT NETANYAHU PROTESTS AHEAD OF NYC VISIT
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian speaks during celebrations marking the 46th anniversary of the 1979 Islamic revolution in Tehran, Iran, on Feb. 10, 2025. (Iranian Presidency/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Meanwhile, Mamdani has said Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City and has called him an "architect" of "genocide." No similar statements about Pezeshkian could be found.
Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani for comment.
National security expert and ACT For America founder Brigitte Gabriel also criticized the mayor over the discrepancy.
Gabriel, who has said she survived a terror attack during the 1975 Lebanese Civil War in Lebanon, now lives in the U.S.
"[The] Iranian President on American soil — while we are still in open conflict with Iran. 18 Americans dead. Thousands of Iranians slaughtered. And he’s getting a visa, a hotel, and a UN microphone in New York," Gabriel fumed on X.
"Where are the war crimes charges? Where’s Mamdani to arrest him while he’s in NYC?"
ISRAEL'S AMBASSADOR SAYS NYC’S MAMDANI IS ‘SOWING CHAOS’ AHEAD OF NETANYAHU’S UN APPEARANCE
Masih Alinejad, a prominent Iranian American human rights activist, attends an interview with the Associated Press in Berlin, Germany, on Nov. 9, 2024. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi, File)
Israeli U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon told reporters Tuesday that Mamdani should stop attacking his nation’s government and turn his attention to Pezeshkian’s administration.
"Focus on the problems of the City of New York and stop with promoting anti-Semitism, stop supporting Hamas , and stop engaging with the Iranian regime," Danon said.
Those comments came weeks after Mamdani’s international affairs liaison sought to arrange a meeting with Iranian U.N. Ambassador Amir-Saeid Iravani .
Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton told Fox News the disparity in Mamdani’s rhetoric is stark.
TRUMP TO MEET WITH MAMDANI IN NEW YORK AMID HIGH-STAKES MIDTERM PUSH
"Is Zohran Mamdani threatening to arrest butchers from Iran who have killed tens of thousands of their own people, or genuine war criminals from other countries?" Cotton, R-Ark., asked.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani meet at Gracie Mansion on Sept. 21, 2026.
"No. The one person he cites is the leader of the Jewish State of Israel."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Mamdani met with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, he said afterward the two leaders will continue to have radically different views on Israel and the conflict in Iran.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

articles.title_orig: Tim Janus, competitive eating champion and ‘The Amazing Race’ competitor, dead at 49
articles.title_zh: Tim Janus, competitive eating champion and ‘The Amazing Race’ competitor, dead at 49
articles.content_orig:
Tim Janus, the world champion competitive eater known as “Eater X” who competed alongside Joey Chestnut, has died at age 49.
Janus, who lived in the East Village in NYC, died on Sept. 16 following a long battle with cancer, per Major League Eating.
He peaked at the No. 2 ranking in the world as a competitive eater, behind only Chestnut, who he teamed with on “The Amazing Race 30” in 2017, coming in fifth place.
Janus held titles in tiramisu eating, ramen eating, nigiri sushi eating and burping.
He was also a regular at the Nathan’s Hot Dog Eating Contest, where he finished second to Chestnut in 2010 and third to him in 2014.
Janus was committed to eating anything.
“I’d eat a roll of pennies if I thought I could set a world record, taste doesn’t matter,” he told Food Republic in 2015. “I’d like to eat everything in the world at least once. I’d eat alien if we could find it. If we could raise dinosaurs, I’d sign up to eat those.”
Janus’ career lasted from 2006-18 and he was later inducted into the Major League Eating Hall of Fame.
His signature look on stage was a painted Viking mask face, inspired by his love of wrestling as a child.
“I tell people that I learned a lot about life by eating hot dogs, and I mean it,” he said at his induction. “If you care about something and work hard at it, it makes you better.”
According to the Daily Mail, Janus tweeted in 2016 that he feared the impact competitive eating would have on his body.
“Deep down I’ve wondered how long-term stupid competing is for my health. I can’t ignore that feeling anymore,” he wrote. “For me it’s more about how we’re destroying our bodies. Each of us only gets one,”
Janus retired from the sport two years later and was accepted by the United States Foreign Service, though those plans were halted when he was diagnosed with cancer.
“Tim followed his own passions and dreams without regard for the pressures or expectations of society,” recalled Crazy Legs Conti, Janus’s ex-roommate and former world oyster-eating champion.
“He was unique, brilliant, and beloved by his friends. He lived his life on his own terms.”

articles.title_orig: ‘Dammit, something has to happen’: White House preparing plan for 90-day diesel exports ban
articles.title_zh: ‘Dammit, something has to happen’: White House preparing plan for 90-day diesel exports ban
articles.content_orig:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright, speaking on Wednesday at the Climate Forward live event in Manhattan, dismissed reports that President Trump was preparing a total ban on U.S. exports of diesel in a bid to lower energy prices before the midterm elections. He also said high oil prices “will fade” as the war in Iran is resolved.
The remarks were part of a series of expansive conversations with officials and industry leaders who are wrestling with rising energy costs and a wave of new data centers that have led to a widespread backlash. As the war in Iran has driven up oil and gas prices and shifted the geopolitics of energy, a flurry of start-ups are scrambling to tap into what could be new sources of clean, limitless power.
The day of live journalism came at an enormously consequential moment. Global temperatures continue to rise swiftly , as fossil fuel emissions continue unabated. The war in Iran has upended global energy markets and sparked protests over rising prices worldwide. And a powerful El Niño event is scrambling weather patterns and fueling more extreme weather.
Here’s what the other speakers addressed:
Kate Marvel , who resigned this year from her position as a climate scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies, discussed the effects of losing scientific research and the fallout from the Trump administration eliminating thousands of research positions. Read more ›
Chris Levesque , the chief executive of TerraPower, a nuclear energy company that recently received approval for the first new U.S. commercial reactor in a decade, said his company can build faster and safer nuclear power. “We imagine future plants will take 36 months or less,” he said. Read more ›
Josh Parker : The head of sustainability at the chipmaker Nvidia said artificial intelligence has “huge potential to drive net emissions reductions” but didn’t offer much detail about how or when these reductions would happen. He said A.I.-driven energy savings in manufacturing, buildings and transportation could help cancel out the technology’s carbon footprint. Read more ›
Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia : The Democratic governor said states should do more to regulate A.I. data centers, though she stopped short of endorsing a moratorium. “While ultimately the decision needs to live with the locality,” she said that “the state has a role in creating the real rules of the road.” Read more ›
Jane Fonda: The longtime environmental activist and actor said we are facing two existential crises, climate and democracy, “and they’re completely interconnected.” She assailed the political establishment over inaction on climate change and reflected on her lifetime of activism. Read more ›
Gerard Barron , chief executive of The Metals Company, defended the environmental effects of mining the sea floor after the Trump administration granted its first-ever licenses to do so in the face of a multifaceted pushback. “You have to take into perspective where we’re getting these metals today,” he said. Read more ›
Mary Powell , the chief executive of Sunrun, a solar power company, discussed why Americans are buying solar panels to power their homes and the challenges the industry faces. Sunrun is expecting to see a roughly 10 percent growth in sales activity this year — a notable exception in a struggling industry. Read more ›
Katie White : The British minister for climate transition addressed energy security and the country’s ambition to achieve net zero, subjects that were particularly top of mind after a scorching summer in Britain. “It was a real wake-up call in terms of where we are,” she said. Read more ›
Tim Latimer: Mr. Latimer, the chief executive officer of Fervo Energy, a company that uses oil and gas drilling techniques to pull heat from the Earth, discussed how the technology has escaped the partisan politics of energy. Read more ›
Erin Brockovich and Justin J. Pearson: Ms. Brockovich, the longtime activist, and Mr. Pearson, a Tennessee state representative, encouraged communities to keep up their fights against data centers. “I’ve never seen a scale this big,” Ms. Brockovich said, when asked to compare the backlash against data centers to her previous activism. “You’re just watching a whole country kind of change and rise up and speak up and push back.” Read more ›
The Climate Forward newsletter: Here is how to sign up. (For yesterday’s newsletter, we spoke to António Guterres, the outgoing secretary general of the United Nations, who issued a dire warning about the future of the fight against climate change.)
One of the most prominent climate scientists to resign from the federal government during the second Trump administration described the “chaotic” conditions inside NASA that led to her departure.
“It is not knowing if you are going to have a job the next day. It’s not knowing where your funding is going to come from,” Kate Marvel, who resigned in March from NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies, said. “It’s not being able to plan ahead to hire staff, to buy computing equipment, to design research projects, because that can be taken away in an instant because you used the wrong word.”
Dr. Marvel is one of more than 10,000 workers with doctorates in science and related fields who have left or been fired from federal agencies since last year. Earlier, the Trump administration had canceled the lease of the Goddard Institute’s Manhattan office, a decision that left employees working from home or out of coffee shops.
“It really grieved me to say that I can’t do science because I work at NASA,” Dr. Marvel said of the difficulties she faced in conducting research near the end of her tenure. “What a thing to say. And so I decided to leave. And honestly, who leaves NASA? It’s a dream job. It’s the coolest government agency in the entire world.”
Dr. Marvel now works at Project Drawdown, a nonprofit organization that promotes science-based solutions for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
While she is happy in her new job, she said it was harder to obtain access to certain resources than it was as a federal scientist, such as computing time on the powerful supercomputers that are used to conduct experiments with climate models.
She said she also missed the opportunity to think about some of the ambitious questions that fall under NASA’s purview: “What should big moonshot projects of the future look like?”
As greenhouse gas emissions continue to climb and global temperatures reach new heights, Dr. Marvel said humanity’s efforts to slow climate change remained vital. In the coming months, a powerful El Niño ocean pattern promises to bring a slew of weather hazards whose effects will be intensified by the human-warmed climate.
When asked about a memo last year by the Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates discouraging what he called a “doomsday outlook” on climate change, Dr. Marvel sighed.
“I think that this next year is going to really rub it in Bill Gates’s face, which unfortunately is also going to rub it in the rest of our faces,” she said. “We may be done with talking about climate change. We may be bored of it. But climate change is not bored of us.”
Nuclear power plants are notoriously expensive and slow to build. Only two have been built from scratch in the United States in the last three decades, and they took 11 years to get up and running .
But Chris Levesque, chief executive of the nuclear start-up TerraPower, said the advanced reactors his company is developing can be built much faster.
“We imagine future plants will take 36 months or less,” Mr. Levesque said.
TerraPower, which was founded by Bill Gates in 2006, is one of several companies trying to revive nuclear energy in the United States by building smaller, advanced reactors that are meant to be easier to build than the giant reactors of old. The start-up received federal approval earlier this year to begin construction of its first nuclear power plant near Kemmerer, Wyo.

articles.title_orig: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
articles.title_zh: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
articles.content_orig:
The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House will be in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be lifted immediately.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” lawyers for CNN, Politico and MS NOW said in a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing.
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court.
The news organizations are scheduled to make their case to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly at a 3:30 p.m. ET hearing.
Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing said.
On Tuesday, the White House Press Office sent letters to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” the department said in the filing. The letters also were filed in court.
The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia.
In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said.
The outlets did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment on the allegations in the filing.
Ahead of the court hearing, more than four dozen media outlets and groups filed a friend of the court brief urging the judge to side with the banned outlets. NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, was among the groups that took part in the brief.
The administration’s reason for the ban, the filing said, was “transparently viewpoint discriminatory.”
“The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene,” the group wrote in the filing.
Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta.
In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump said Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets, and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday.
The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.”
Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday, and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said.
He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.”
“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.
The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.”
The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says.
CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says.
The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” their court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.”
“When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.”
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation.
MS NOW is a rotating member of the secondary pool, while Politico is a member of the rotating print pool.
CNN had been scheduled to be the pool camera Monday, and the other networks in the TV network pool jointly declined to step in and replace its coverage, resulting in Trump’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the White House being inaudible.
His remarks at the United Nations on Tuesday and alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a press conference Monday were picked up by U.N. cameras and local news outlets, respectively.
Trump defended the bans in a social media statement Monday and added a new argument — that “fake news” is a national security issue.
“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
