articles.title_orig: NFL Fantasy 2026 Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Quarterbacks for Week 3
articles.title_zh: NFL Fantasy 2026 Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Quarterbacks for Week 3
articles.content_orig:
NFL Fantasy 2026 Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Quarterbacks for Week 3
As always, Start 'Em, Sit 'Em is geared toward helping fantasy managers make difficult roster decisions. You won’t see “start Jahmyr Gibbs” here. Instead, I'm exploring the players closer to the perceived fringe and aiming to optimize your lineup for a win each week. Importantly, the new “Start of the Week” and “Sit of the Week” are the calls I have deemed the most notable in each category, not necessarily the most essential players to start or sit.
Also, you’ll see quite a few references in this year’s column to NFL Pro, spotlighting insights provided through Next Gen Stats data dashboards, matchup evaluations, All-22 film and the uniquely trained Fantasy AI Assistant. You can get access to all of those tools yourself with an NFL+ Premium subscription!
P.S. Feel free to follow me on X (@MattOkada) or Instagram (@mattokadaNFL) and hit me with your questions, congratulations or complaints throughout the year.
Hear me out. Despite being unexpectedly thrown into action just a few snaps into the 2026 season, Lock has been undeniably efficient through two weeks in Seattle. He ranks top five in passer rating (127.3), yards per attempt (8.8), completion rate (72.9%), completion rate over expected (8.8%), EPA/dropback (0.44), and is one of three quarterbacks (alongside Josh Allen and Jared Goff) with at least four touchdown passes and zero interceptions. In Week 3, Lock draws a Commanders defense that’s allowed the highest passer rating, most touchdown passes and second-most fantasy points to the position. He’s a lock -- pun intended -- for QB1 production on Sunday.
While nearly everything has looked off for the Chargers' offense, Herbert will need to air it out in this matchup. I believe he'll log his first strong fantasy performance of 2026 against a D that gave up multiple touchdown passes to C.J Stroud (2) and Jared Goff (4) over the past two weeks.
Goff is fifth in fantasy points among quarterbacks through two weeks and is back at home -- where he typically thrives -- against a beatable Jets defense. Expect another multi-TD performance from the reliable QB1.
Don’t look now, but Shough leads the NFL in completions (62) and passing yards (662). The Raiders might be a sneaky-tough matchup, but they’ve also faced Malik Willis and a dysfunctional Chargers offense. Shough is streamable in a pinch.
Through two weeks, Smith has a 95.8 passer rating and 70.8% completion rate, while the Lions have allowed a league-high 64.02 fantasy points to quarterbacks (Tyler Shough and Josh Allen). Smith is viable as a (deep) streamer.
We knew Stafford and the Rams would turn it around sooner than later ... but dang! He dropped 26.98 fantasy points without Puka Nacua on Monday night. Denver's definitely a tough matchup, but you can play the reigning MVP regardless.
There’s no sugarcoating it: Maye has not looked good through two weeks. He’s tied with Cooper Rush for the league lead in interceptions and all four of Maye’s picks have come on deep throws, resulting in a 45.8 passer rating and -0.73 EPA/dropback on such passes. In contrast, Maye threw just one INT and recorded a league-high 1.23 EPA/dropback on 48 deep passes last season. The Jaguars' defense hasn’t been unbeatable, but that unit doesn't grant any extra confidence in Maye’s Week 3 outlook, either. He’s benchable for a strong stream like Drew Lock or Jared Goff.
Mayfield has been disappointing, and he’s unlikely to be much better against Brian Flores’ defense despite this game being played at home. Minnesota is second in pressure rate (49.4%) and Mayfield is not a storied blitz-beater.
Hopes that Jones would quickly return to his early-2025 excellence have been quickly dashed this season. He has averaged 12.22 fantasy points per game, receiver Alec Pierce just hit injured reserve and now the Texans' defense is coming to town. Absolute must-sit material.
Love is dead last in completion rate (52.1%) and 15th in fantasy points among qualified quarterbacks. I fear his meeting with Atlanta will look more like Aaron Rodgers’ (12.54 fantasy points vs. the Falcons in Week 1) than Bryce Young’s (24.08 in Week 2). Avoid him if possible.

Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
Trump lawyers say White House access is ‘a privilege, not a right’; CNN, Politico and MS Now to present case in court after president banned outlets from White House grounds
Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.
Trump administration drafting up plans for 90-day embargo on diesel exports: report
The Trump administration is readying to launch a 90-day ban on diesel fuel exports from the United States, following mounting calls from his party to take action to bring down the fuel’s price ahead of the midterm elections, POLITICO reported Wednesday.
Several people with inside knowledge of the conversations told POLITICO (currently one of three outlets banned from the White House by Trump) that the plan has created a schism within pro- and anti-embargo camps in the administration. It’s also prompted furor from the oil and gas industry that has broadly supported the president.
One oil industry executive privy to the conversations told the outlet that Trump seemed intent on announcing a ban by the end of the week.
The price of fuel has weighed heavily on Republicans in the lead-up to the midterms, which will determine whether Trump’s party retains control of Congress for the second half of his term. Trump ran in 2024 in part on bringing down the price of gas, but the war he helped kick off between the US and Iran, and the closure of vital oil shipping arteries it prompted, has sent the cost of fuel skyrocketing.
Diesel, in particular, has become a sore spot. The fuel for everything from semi-trucks to tractors to heavy machinery, it has surged in price even more than standard gasoline, to more than $6.50 per gallon.
That’s prompted some Republicans, especially those representing farming-heavy states, to publicly call on the president to take drastic action to lower the price of diesel.
The pushback, POLITICO reports, is coming from oil and gas executives and administration officials who warn that the embargo could raise fuel prices in the long run.
Yesterday, Britain’s new prime minister Andy Burnham navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with DonaldTrump at the UN general assembly in New York. His aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a “natural businessman”.
The anticipated sticking points – theChagos Islands, WestBank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to the our policy editor in London, Kiran Stacey. You can also watch on YouTube.
'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team.”
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.
Rubio, in his press conference, also touched on the war in Iran at several points, including on the surprise negotiations that took place yesterday between Trump administration envoys and the Iran delegation.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough,” Rubio said. “But at the same time I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”
Little detail has been shared about what was discussed at that meetings, though Rubio framed the conversation as a continuation of the earlier back-and-forth between the two sides.
Rubio also notably insisted that Trump would be able to see through his campaign in Iran acting on his authority alone, even if Republicans lose control of Congress in November and if Democrats were to oppose the continuation of US operations against the country.
Rubio also briefly addressed Trump’s meeting with Delcy Rodriguez, the interim Venezuelan president, who last night posed for a friendly photo with Trump at a Manhattan hotel only miles from where her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was incarcerated.
“It was a short meeting, but it was a very important meeting,” Rubio said.

articles.title_orig: Son of Israeli ambassador to US critically injured in West Bank ramming attack
articles.title_zh: Son of Israeli ambassador to US critically injured in West Bank ramming attack
articles.content_orig:
The son of Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter was critically injured in a ramming attack in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday afternoon, according to regional authorities, one day before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s scheduled speech at the United Nations.
Neria Leiter, a reserve soldier manning a checkpoint near the settlement of Beit Horon, was rushed to a hospital in Jerusalem, according to emergency response services.
“Neria needs a miracle,” Leiter said in a statement on social media. “I believe in the power of prayer, and I believe that when the people of Israel unite, miracles happen.”
The driver of the car, 29-year-old Mahmoud Muhammad Mahmoud Suleiman, a Palestinian from the nearby village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, was shot and killed at the scene of the attack, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Hamas praised the attack in a statement Wednesday, describing it as a “natural response” to Israeli actions in the West Bank and Jerusalem. The militant group in the Gaza Strip called for increased resistance against Israel but did not claim responsibility for the attack.
Leiter’s elder son, 39-year-old Moshe Yedidya Leiter, was killed fighting in Gaza in November 2023 in the first weeks of the war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel the month before.
The ramming attack occurred just days after a shooting in the West Bank on the eve of the Jewish high holiday of Yom Kippur. On Sunday morning, Netanel Shukrun, a father of six from the settlement of Alei Zahav, was shot and killed while bathing at a natural spring in the West Bank as part of the holiday customs. Shukrun’s 16-year-old son credited his father with saving his life when he shouted out a warning to take cover.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) arrested the suspected shooter at a hospital near the West Bank city of Ramallah, the military said Sunday. Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the death penalty in the case under a new law applying capital punishment to terrorism and nationalistic murders.
After the shooting, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the IDF chief of staff, said: “The IDF is on high alert, deployed and prepared with soldiers reinforced across all sectors, including throughout the fast. Our mission is clear and ongoing — to thwart terrorism, act decisively against every threat, and protect the citizens of the State of Israel.”
Since October 7, 2023, Israel has carried out waves of widescale military operations in the West Bank intended to target what officials view as centers of terrorist activity. The operations have led to the displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians across the territory and military raids into Palestinian villages.
“Terrorism currently in Judea and Samaria is at its lowest level in decades,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said in early September, using the biblical name for the West Bank, “and we will take all necessary steps to prevent terrorism from rearing its head again.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.title_zh: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.content_orig:
Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
The EU Industry Commissioner warned that the EU will consider using punitive trade measures if Beijing does not rebalance the trade deficit, which costs the bloc thousands of jobs every week.
The European Union "urgently" needs to act quickly to rebalance its "unsustainable" trade relationship with China, Commission Executive Vice-President for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, Stéphane Séjourné, told Euronews, stressing that significant job losses are at stake.
Recent customs data showed the gap between the bloc's imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1 billion a day in July.
"This trade rebalancing is becoming existential for Europeans," Séjourné said on Euronews' interview programme The Europe Conversation.
"Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," he noted, adding that the EU already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year. These were particularly concentrated in energy-intensive sectors and automotive supply chains. "It's urgent that we act, and urgent that we rebalance."
The EU, meanwhile, began crucial negotiations with Beijing in June this year, and has set a looming October deadline for concrete, "credible" outcomes. This will culminate in a high-stakes visit by EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to Beijing on 8 and 9 October, where Brussels is hoping to secure commitments from China that it will curb exports to the EU.
"The European Commission has put forward a proposal to the Chinese side to discuss this sector by sector and look at how we can rebalance things," Séjourné said. "This imbalance isn't sustainable, not for China or for the EU."
However, so far, Beijing has been resisting calls from the Europeans, pushing back against calls for voluntary export curbs.
The EU Industry Commissioner said that negotiation and discussion will be "given a chance," but that the Commission has been clear on the consequences of talks not producing the results.
"Trade defence tools are on the table," he warned. "Today we need credibility in how we use these tools, and we won't hesitate to use them to rebalance things."
Tools currently on the table include anti-dumping duties and tariffs against unfair subsidies (in industries such as electric vehicles and solar panels).
But Brussels is walking a tightrope when it comes to defending the EU market, as Chinese retaliation could see the country restrict exports of rare earths, essential to several of the EU's key industries, including defence.
The EU will also be keeping its eye on talks between Washington and Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping is landing in the United States for a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump, which is set to cover issues ranging from trade to AI and rare earths.
The outcome of these talks between the two economic superpowers could directly affect Europe's economic interests, Séjourné explained.
"We need a constructive dialogue between China and the United States. As we saw last year, the trade escalation between Washington and Beijing on these issues could spark a trade war, one that could even affect the European economy."
Last year, an explosive tit-for-tat trade war saw the US and China hike tariffs on each other's goods to dizzying heights. At the peak of this battle, the US imposed 145% tariffs on Chinese imports, while Beijing's retaliatory duties reached 125%.
For Europe, a trade war between the US and China hits hard, as astronomical tariffs on China inevitably lead to the diversion of Chinese goods from the US to the EU.
On the agenda this week in the US will be the looming expiration of the trade truce, due to expire on 10 November.
"I hope this dialogue can be constructive, that an agreement can be reached, and that the situation can be stabilised," Séjourné concluded.

articles.title_orig: No first-year coach has won the Super Bowl in 37 years. Can Jesse Minter, steadfast and steady, change that?
articles.title_zh: No first-year coach has won the Super Bowl in 37 years. Can Jesse Minter, steadfast and steady, change that?
articles.content_orig:
For month after bleary-eyed month this offseason, Jesse Minter did everything he could to succeed as a first-year head coach. So as the final moments ticked away in the Ravens' 41-23 Week 1 win over the Colts -- Minter's first victory -- he could finally take a breath and celebrate.
A hug from Lamar Jackson, the quarterback he won over with an in-home visit weeks after being hired. An embrace from his dad, longtime coach Rick Minter, now on Baltimore's staff. He knew he and his team had so far to go, but he could savor this.
"It's surreal a little bit, honestly. I don't know if it has actually hit me yet," Minter said.
That's fair. It's been quite the journey.
The setbacks that made Minter a coach
Getting to where Jesse Minter is today, like any of the 32 NFL head coaches, required a lot of hard work, a lot of luck and a few good breaks.
And for Minter, it required, quite literally, a bad break.
After starting college at Cincinnati, where his father, Rick, was the coach, Jesse transferred to Division III Mount St. Joseph, where he could play football.
"When he came in with his dad, it was so obvious that he was dying to play the game," former Mount St. Joseph coach Rob Huber told CBS Sports. "... It was a no-brainer."
But Minter broke his leg in his first season. He had emergency surgery for Crohn's disease -- 18 inches of his colon removed, per The Athletic -- and missed the entire next season. He suffered another leg fracture in his third year.
He could have slunk away. Plenty have; plenty will. Minter did the opposite.
"There's a lot of guys that, when they get injured and things like that, they sort of detach themselves from the team," says Volker, who was a college teammate of Minter. "I feel like he got even more involved. He really embraced that role wholeheartedly."
That meant the unglamorous work of being a de facto assistant coach at a D-III program. Minter drove for hours to pick up grainy VHS game film from opponents and broke that film down on a TV he had to roll onto wrestling mats; Mount St. Joseph's football and wrestling teams shared several common areas. He lugged himself around, boot or crutches be damned, into cramped coaching boxes, crowded sidelines and overflowing buses. He did it all while working tirelessly to get back onto the field, too.
"As far as his mental, physical toughness, he's without a doubt the toughest person I've ever coached in 40 years," Huber said.
The setbacks on the field proved a launching pad into coaching. Huber, with just two full-time assistants, was more than happy to have a player who had been around coaches his whole life join the extended staff.
"What really was, I think, a big part of this is how serious our coaches took him," said Andy Wellendorf, a fellow wide receiver at Mount St. Joseph and a close friend ever since. "I think there were 120 guys on our roster. I think if 119 people were in his spot, nobody would have taken it seriously."
When he lost the ability to play, Minter found his voice as a coach.
"Talking to the big groups, the team, when we have 120 kids in the locker room, and he's the one communicating with the team, that was impressive to me," Wellendorf said. "It's hard to grab the attention of 120 college-age guys, right? But it's like, 'No, we're going to do it when Jesse's talking. He's got something to say, so we're going to listen to him.'"
Mt. Saint Joseph was 0-10 in 2001, the year before Minter arrived. It went 10-0 in the regular season in 2004, Minter and Wellendorf's junior year.
"He was a big part of the run, man," Huber said. "Everybody loved Jesse Minter."
Upon graduating, Minter took a defensive intern role at Notre Dame -- Rick Minter was the defensive coordinator -- in 2006. Both got fired at season's end.
Rick knew then-Cincinnati coach Brian Kelly and still had the number for the landline in the head coach's office -- Rick's old office -- as Minter told The Athletic last year. The cold call worked. Jesse got a job as a graduate assistant, specifically working with the linebackers. His role featured computer, data and film duties and helping with the scout team, but he impressed Kelly with his on-field, hands-on teaching technique, too.
"I really enjoyed him being around us, because he is like he is today," Kelly said. "He has this approach that is disarming in so many ways, but yet he's detailed and organized, and I could see as a young coach, he was meant to be leading men."
He'd get that opportunity soon enough: After 2008, his second year with the Bearcats, Indiana State head coach Trent Miles offered Minter the Sycamores' linebackers coach position.
"He came in and said, 'Coach, what do you think?' Kelly recalls. "I said, 'You need to take the job.'"
Minter would become defensive coordinator two years later and serve as the architect behind some of the program's biggest wins.
The game that showed what Minter could build
Take Oct. 12, 2012, for example. The biggest thing Indiana State linebackers coach P.J. Volker notices is how calm the defense is.
Indiana State -- a program that went 2-54 from 2005-09 and seemed, at times, on the brink of going under -- was a day away from facing FCS reigning champion and No. 1-ranked North Dakota State in the Fargodome. The Sycamores' defenders had every right to be nervous. They also had the coordinator to ensure they wouldn't be.
Minter, all of 29 years old and in his second year as the Sycamores' defensive coordinator, had a plan and a belief it would work -- a belief he instilled in his players, too.
"I really remember the night before the game how relaxed our guys were, because that's how Jesse was," Volker, now the Ravens' safeties coach, told CBS Sports. There was no doubt in my mind, and I think everybody's mind on our defense, that we were going to go out and play phenomenal football."
The plan emphasized stopping the power run game to put North Dakota State in third and longs. On third downs, the Sycamores would bring pressure up front with complex, rotating coverages behind it.
"What I remember from it is just going into the game with a lot of confidence in our game plan," Ben Obaseki, a defensive lineman on that team, told CBS Sports.
It worked. Indiana State's defense was the offense, too ± two pick-sixes -- and had a third interception late to seal a 17-14 upset. It was the fewest points the Bison had scored at home in seven years. The Sycamores landed home in Terre Haute to fans celebrating the school's first win over a No. 1-ranked team.
"It was a fun flight home," Miles told CBS Sports. "I can't remember too much about it. That was a long time ago, man, and I'm getting up there, but I tell you, we didn't go to sleep right away when we got home."
It was one of several wins from Miles that caught the eye of Georgia State, which was entering its first year as an FBS program. When the school offered Miles the head coaching position, Miles brought Minter with him to Atlanta, and the Panthers went from winless in 2013 to a bowl team in 2015. The defense was even better -- top-10 passing yards per game allowed in 2016 -- but Miles got fired midseason, and Minter soon followed.
Minter then jumped to the NFL in 2017 thanks to another connection -- John Harbaugh had been Rick Minter's special teams coach -- and became a defensive assistant for Baltimore. He got promoted to defensive backs coach in 2020. When COVID-19 put the world on pause and, months later, offenses exploded around the NFL, Minter did some of his finest work. The Ravens were second in the league in yards per pass attempt allowed.
Then it was back to college, as Vanderbilt's defensive coordinator in 2021 and as Michigan's in 2022 and 2023, when the Wolverines won a national championship and led FBS in total defense. Jim Harbaugh brought him along to the Chargers, and after two terrific years, he landed the top job in Baltimore, where he's trying to do something that hasn't been done since 1990.
A different kind of opportunity in Baltimore

articles.title_orig: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China’s lunar “exploration” plans
articles.title_zh: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China’s lunar “exploration” plans
articles.content_orig:
In a forthcoming memoir, former US politician and NASA Administrator Bill Nelson offers a blistering assessment of China, saying the United States must do all it can to retain its leadership in space exploration.
“Beijing’s intended strategy is to dominate the high ground of the twenty-first century,” writes Nelson in Space Odyssey, a book to be published by Harper Horizon in January 2027.
A former Congressman and Senator from Florida, Nelson served as a mission specialist on a space shuttle flight in 1986 and later as NASA administrator from May 2021 to January 2025 under President Biden. The book largely focuses on his space policy work in Congress and his tenure as NASA’s leader.
Nelson recounts how in early 2023, NASA assisted the US military when a Chinese spy balloon began traversing the United States. With its experience in using balloons to map the stratosphere and model atmospheric currents, NASA provided information on how to shoot the balloon down without endangering anyone on the ground.
He argues that the balloon saga offered further affirmation that the United States was enmeshed in a high-stakes competition with China for the high ground.
“What many Americans first registered as a balloon violating our airspace was really a warning that the next great rivalry will not be fought on land or sea but the skies above us and even beyond our atmosphere,” he writes. “The episode was also a window into the new space race that is swiftly approaching its most urgent phase, with the stakes even higher than the Cold War contest.”
Nelson has long been wary of China as a threat to the United States, noting his concerns about technology theft from the West. Unlike his predecessor under a Democratic president—former astronaut Charlie Bolden, who served as NASA leader under President Obama—Nelson supported the Wolf Amendment, which strictly limits cooperation between NASA and China’s space program.

articles.title_orig: Trump invites Putin to G20 in Miami, Rubio says
articles.title_zh: Trump invites Putin to G20 in Miami, Rubio says
articles.content_orig:
The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York.
“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”
The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies.
Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club.
Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”.
The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries.
European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit.
Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended.
“We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.”
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy addressed the United Nations, urging world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war effort.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelenskyy. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.”
Zelenskyy also warned that the war could spread beyond Ukraine if Putin was not stopped.
Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”.
Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices.
In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress.
Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy.
“President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet.
For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens.
On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke.
A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station.
Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well.
In response to what has happened, the House foreign affairs committee posted on X: “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.”
Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv

articles.title_orig: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.title_zh: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.content_orig:
America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
Long-standing educational programs such as Fulbright, Boren, and the Critical Language Scholarship are all suspended. A leader-level deal could bring them back and protect the students who take part.
- Rosie LevineExecutive Director of the U.S.-China Education Trust
- Rush DoshiCFR ExpertC.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia Studies and Director of the China Strategy Initiative
Derk Bodde set out for Beijing in 1948 expecting to spend a quiet year translating an esoteric work of Chinese philosophy. Instead, as the first recipient of the newly created Fulbright fellowship in China, he found himself an eyewitness to the Chinese Communist Party’s takeover, and his account of what he saw became a rare firsthand record for policymakers, academics, and the American public. When China closed to foreign contact for the next quarter-century, Bodde’s expertise didn’t just remain useful: it was irreplaceable.
Bodde’s story is a clear example of the ways in which in-country research is a proven and often indispensable tool to strengthen American expertise of foreign countries—and not only with friendly nations. But as Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare to meet tomorrow in Washington, DC, only around two thousand Americans are studying in China, down from fifteen thousand a decade ago, and the public and private ecosystem that once supported deep American study of China is collapsing precisely when it is needed most.
That decline is due both to funding cuts and legitimate concerns that students may face risks of arbitrary detention in China. Currently, two American academics have been designated as wrongfully detained after traveling to China for academic purposes, creating risks that must be addressed by Beijing. Such cases are rare—the vast majority of Americans who study in China do so without incident—but they are real, and their chilling effect reaches far beyond the individuals involved. At the upcoming summit, Presidents Trump and President Xi should elevate specific programs like Fulbright into leader-level deliverables, with President Xi’s high-profile support for them at the summit providing implicit assurances that participants will not face undue risks from China’s security services.
This approach has some precedent. Exchange programs sometimes receive broad protections from leaders. Indeed, even at the height of the Cold War, the United States established the International Research and Exchanges Board (IREX) in 1968 as a formalized, bilateral academic exchange mechanism, sending generations of American Sovietologists into the Soviet Union, even as the two countries remained locked in rivalry. IREX and its successors, including the Committee on Scholarly Communication with the People’s Republic of China, which managed similar style exchanges with China before diplomatic normalization, were established to lend U.S. government protection to academic exchanges deemed essential to the national interest.
By contrast, the China programs that built a generation of expertise are now defunct. The Fulbright Program has been suspended in China since 2020, partly over risks that participating students and researchers might be detained by China. Alongside Fulbright, less well-known but essential U.S. government–funded programs specifically designed to encourage greater foreign area expertise in government have been suspended to mainland China, including the Boren Awards, the Critical Language Scholarship, the National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI-Y), and more.
At home, the area studies infrastructure in U.S. universities that was built in the 1950s, including the National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and Foreign Language and Area Studies (FLAS) fellowships, has been gutted amid cuts at the Department of Education. In recent weeks, new unclear federal restrictions on higher education’s ties to China have pushed some universities to conclude that even nonsensitive academic engagement—undergraduate study abroad included—carries too much risk: the University of North Carolina is the latest institution to pull down its study abroad program.
Critics of travel to China argue that Taiwan offers a safer alternative for Mandarin language study, and that the extent of state surveillance makes the risk of visiting China not worth the potential benefits. But Taiwan’s educational opportunities, while excellent, cannot fully substitute for the loss of access to China’s economy, society, and culture.
America needs a much deeper supply of China experts to handle a fast-changing relationship. In closed-door meetings compiled for the U.S.-China Education Trust’s 2026 report, America’s China Talent Challenge, stakeholders across the U.S. government, business, and academia described how their sectors depend on American expertise to interpret China’s actions—from geopolitics and security, to trade and supply chains—and to keep the United States competitive. The working group concluded that China expertise must be considered a national resource.
As Trump and Xi meet in Washington, progress on people-to-people diplomacy may be less challenging than in other domains. But both sides can take steps to improve the situation.
First, the Trump administration should negotiate with Beijing to elevate specific programs, from named legacy programs—including the Fulbright, Boren, Critical Language Scholarship, and NSLI-Y—to new initiatives, into summit deliverables. President Xi’s endorsement of these programs would provide implicit protection for those students who participate in them. President Trump could privately push to formalize assurances that participants will face no risks from China’s security services. And to make that gesture credible, Beijing should release detained academics.
Second, in tandem with these negotiations, the United States should reverse cuts to funding programs, which are in many cases entirely unrelated to China. The area studies infrastructure built nearly eighty years ago, to include National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and FLAS fellowships, has been gutted and should be restored. Congress should also fund new programs, purpose-built for today’s U.S.-China relationship. Scrutiny of university ties to China is in some cases warranted, but it should be scoped so that nonsensitive academic engagement, such as undergraduate study abroad and language programs, are able to proceed with appropriate safeguards.
To some, these proposals may seem unrealistic. But they are rooted in history and pragmatism. Washington has long had educational programs in countries with competitors and adversaries. Those programs were often sustained by leader-level understandings that they would be insulated from competitive dynamics in the relationship. Improving mutual understanding is inherently valuable. For both Washington and Beijing, it also reduces the risk of miscalculation. If the next generation of policymakers has no China experience, both countries will suffer.
A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, or track policy implementation on the ground is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable. Rebuilding China expertise is not an act of goodwill toward Beijing. It is a hard-nosed investment in the United States’ atrophying ability to understand and compete with its most consequential rival.
The United States and China have few bright spots in the bilateral relationship, and fewer still that could be elevated into summit deliverables. Naming and insulating a handful of exchange programs from political and security pressures is in fact one of the most straightforward areas for cooperation that exists between the two countries.

articles.title_orig: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Jimmy Garoppolo and 4 other QBs who could help teams in need - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Jimmy Garoppolo and 4 other QBs who could help teams in need - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Five plays into the 2026 NFL season, we saw the first starting quarterback go down.
The Seattle Seahawks' Sam Darnold suffered a glute injury against the New England Patriots, and just like that, Drew Lock was leading the defending Super Bowl champs to a comeback victory on Opening Night.
It wouldn't take much longer for more starting quarterbacks to fall.
Less than 10 minutes into his Vikings debut in Week 1, Kyler Murray was knocked out with a concussion. Week 2 saw three recent first-round quarterbacks succumb to injury: Chicago's Caleb Williams and Washington's Jayden Daniels, the first two picks of the 2024 NFL Draft, followed by the Giants' Jaxson Dart — and each injury seemingly worse than the next.
Along with the Atlanta Falcons, who were forced to start Cooper Rush the first two games ahead of either Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr., it's fair to say that the starting-quarterback injury epidemic is already raging after two weeks. Nearly 20% of the league has been forced to play backup QBs, with almost 90% of the regular season still remaining.
Backups clearly matter. Brock Purdy missed almost half the 2025 regular season, but Mac Jones helped keep the 49ers afloat. When C.J. Stroud missed three games last season, Texans backup Davis Mills went 3-0 in his place, keeping them in the playoff race. But when Patrick Mahomes got hurt, the drop-off to Gardner Minshew — and later Chris Oladokun — was too steep for the Chiefs to survive.
Some teams, we're finding out, have protected their most important assets better than others. Here's how we'd rank the six teams that have needed to dip into their QB reserves:
6) Tua Tagovailoa/Michael Penix Jr./Cooper Rush/Jack Strand, Atlanta Falcons
Who's the starter? Who's the backup? It's often not a pretty situation when those two questions aren't followed by easy answers.
The Falcons have the toughest situation of the lot right now, even with the most theoretical options. Tagovailoa was nominally the starter until he got hurt; Penix, the logical replacement, couldn't go the first two weeks.
That left the reins to Rush, who struggled in Baltimore last season and who did little in his two starts this season in leading the Falcons to an 0-2 start. Strand, the Division-II prospect who had an encouraging preseason, replaced Rush in Week 2 and threw a pick-6 on his first NFL pass attempt.
Clearly the hope is that the often-injured Penix can step in now, having been named Atlanta's Week 3 starter, and run with the job. The Falcons have little other hope, short of (the also often-injured) Tagovailoa returning to action.
Until proven otherwise, Kevin Stefanski has the same issue in Atlanta that he had in Cleveland: quarterback uncertainty.
5) Jameis Winston, New York Giants
With Jaxson Dart now ruled out for the season, the Giants are in a really tough spot, with no young quarterback to prepare in the wings. Winston has a wealth of experience, with 89 career starts, but as Monday's replacement performance showed, his play can be a wild experience.
Winston struggled against the Rams and has been a turnover machine in his career, with 141 of them (114 INTs, 27 lost fumbles) in 109 career outings. He's had a five-pick game and a three-fumble game. Winston also has five career 400-yard games and two five-TD, no-INT performances. You really never know what you're going to get any given week.
Head coach John Harbaugh has to find another option in case he gets too much bad Winston, with only Jake Haener currently on the practice squad. Some have floated a J.J. McCarthy trade to the Giants, but would that throw only more gas on the fire?
4) Tyson Bagent/Case Keenum, Chicago Bears
This pairing could arguably be higher on the list, but Bagent's concussion (which might have come on the final play Sunday) could keep him out of Monday night's game against the Philadelphia Eagles, which would give Keenum his first start — and his first regular-season action — since 2023.
Bagent has barely seen the field since Caleb Williams was drafted, but he started four games in 2023 and replaced Williams for the final two drives Sunday. His body of work is incomplete, but Bagent possesses intriguing skills and it wouldn't be shocking if he led a team at starter level for a stretch.
It's unclear how long Williams will be out, but for the first time since he came to Chicago, the Bears will have to lean on his replacements.
3) Drew Lock/Jalen Milroe, Seattle Seahawks
Lock came in cold in Week 1 and did just enough to help the Seahawks win, settling down after a few shaky patches. Then he came out guns blazing in Week 2, throwing for three TDs. Would you believe that Lock leads the NFL in passer rating through two games? He entered the season completing fewer than 60% of his career passes but is sitting at 72.7% in 2026.
If Lock, who turns 30 in November, can continue to fill in ably for the injured Darnold, it's not a stretch to think he could follow the Geno Smith post-30 path of earning his way back into a starting lineup, perhaps as a bridge option for a team that drafts a higher-round QB next spring. It appears that Lock has worked out some of the recklessness in his game and is becoming more dependable.
Milroe remains a curiosity with strong physical skills, but he's still virtually unknown. His best shot might be to continue working behind the scenes and vie for Lock's QB2 spot next season.
2) Carson Wentz/J.J. McCarthy, Minnesota Vikings
Wentz might be known in some circles as a bust, or as the guy whose team went on to win a Super Bowl after he got hurt. Even still, he's carved out a career for himself as an able QB2, willing and ready to jump into the fire. He did so early against the Packers when Kyler Murray got hurt, leading the Vikings to a 12-point comeback in the game's final 20 minutes. Then Wentz turned in a solid, turnover-free effort in his Week 2 start against the Bears, leading Minnesota to a shocking 9-3 win and a 2-0 start to the season.
Not bad for a guy who wasn't even part of the Vikings' starting derby in camp. His outing vs. the Bears marked 11 straight seasons with at least one start for Wentz. He'll take a seat again with Murray expected to start in Week 3, but Wentz's contributions can't be forgotten.
McCarthy, who lost the starting battle to Murray, remains an enigma. He's under contract through 2027 with a 2028 option, but the path back to being relevant for this team appears longer and more windy now.
1) Marcus Mariota/Athan Kaliakmanis,
Mariota is in some ways the gold standard of backup quarterbacks, along with the 49ers' Jones. With 82 career starts, Mariota has more experience than many current starters. He stepped in ably for Jayden Daniels in Sunday's loss to the Cowboys, looking sharp, and was competitive during Daniels' two missed stints last season.
With Daniels expected to miss 4-6 weeks with his latest left elbow injury, Mariota will be thrust back onto the saddle as he approaches his 33rd birthday. The biggest benefit is that he can run the same offense Daniels did, with little tweaking necessary.
The rookie Kaliakmanis had a strong preseason, receiving extra reps when Mariota's knee injury flared up and impressing the team with his arm talent and moxie.

Swift went viral for her reaction to Kelce’s first-quarter touchdown in the Kansas City Chiefs’ 33-30 win over the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium when she pointed to her ring. NBC cameras caught Swift yelling in jubilation, "That’s my husband!"
For Kelce, he was doing what he’s supposed to do.

articles.title_orig: 6 people killed in bear attacks in Siberia, as official warns one town is "under siege"
articles.title_zh: 6 people killed in bear attacks in Siberia, as official warns one town is "under siege"
articles.content_orig:
At least six people have been killed in bear attacks in Russia's vast Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk in a month, prosecutors said Wednesday, as an official in a neighboring region reported bears had put one town "under siege."
Prosecutors said they opened a probe into criminal negligence, accusing local officials of failing to control bear numbers.
Russia's brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to Russia's natural resources ministry.
While the number of bear attacks across Russia has remained constant at around 20 to 30 a year, according to the ministry, local media and officials have expressed alarm about the rising numbers. At least 14 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since the start of the year, according to a tally by The Moscow Times .
Despite numerous warnings, local officials "failed to take measures to regulate the predator population or prevent them from appearing in areas inhabited by people," the Investigative Committee of Russia's sparsely populated Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia regions said on its website.
The bodies of two pensioners were found mauled in a forest near the remote town of Podtyosovo earlier this month, followed by the death of a 40-year-old factory worker who walked through the forest on Sept. 6, according to local media.
Earlier this month, two people were killed while foraging for wild berries in a remote forest on the banks of the Lena River, the Moscow Times reported .
"One person managed to escape and report the incident," the regional branch of Russia's Interior Ministry said, according to the outlet.
A 39-year-old logger guarding machinery was killed by a bear in the forest early Wednesday, investigators said.
The deputy head of the neighboring Khakassia region, Dmitry Buchenik, said Wednesday that the forest town of Abaza — home to around 10,000 people — was surrounded by bears "on all sides."
"It was an alarming night in Abaza. The taiga town is effectively under siege by bears," he said.
"Some of the animals were chased off, but three were killed (one of them was huge)," he added.
Unverified social media videos purported to show a bear swimming across a river beside the town, while another showed a group of three bears leaping across a road in front of cars.
Russia's emergency ministry says bears flee in the vast majority of encounters with humans.
Earlier this year, officials said three members of a family, including a child, were injured by a polar bear in a rare attack in the far north of Siberia.

articles.title_orig: Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
articles.title_zh: Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
articles.content_orig:
Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
Global South countries will be worst affected by the phenomenon sweeping the planet from June to February.
The record global heat caused by this year’s powerful “super El Nino” could cause nearly half a million excess deaths worldwide by early next year, according to a report (PDF) published by the global research collaboration, Climate Impact Lab, on Wednesday.
So what does the report reveal, how has climate change supercharged the effects of El Nino and should we all be really worried?
- list 1 of 3UN warns El Nino could be ‘off the charts’, strongest in decades
- list 2 of 3Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
- list 3 of 3El Nino set to be most intense ‘for over a century’: UK forecasters
Climate Impact Lab (CIL)’s report has found that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June this year and the end of February 2027 could be caused by the effects of El Nino, than the number expected in an average year.
The study’s authors came to their projections after researching the relationship between temperature and excess mortality in 24,378 regions, taking local climate and vulnerability into account.
They combined those findings with temperature forecasts to estimate excess deaths which could arise from heat caused by El Nino compared with the 1996-2025 average.
Their methodology will be published in a peer-reviewed journal.
The number of extremely hot days is likely to rise by 44 percent compared with normal years, according to the report, titled, “451,000 at Risk: Where Action Can Save Lives During the Super El Nino”.
The researchers described this year’s El Nino as a “postcard from the future”, ushering in temperatures that will become the new normal in just a few decades.
It recommended that emergency response efforts should be directed to high-priority regions to tackle heat-related mortality in the coming months.
CIL’s Adaptation Inventory recommends implementing a number of measures to help vulnerable populations cope with extreme heat, including issuing heat warnings, increasing the number of staff at medical facilities during the hottest periods, establishing cooling centres where people can shelter and implementing protections for outdoor workers.
“This report allows decision-makers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months,” said Michael Greenstone, economist at the University of Chicago and cofounder of CIL.
El Nino is the period of time during which the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean heats up to at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 degrees Fahrenheit) above average temperatures. It takes place every few years and is part of a natural climate cycle that alternates between a warm phase – El Nino – and a cool phase, known as La Nina.
During El Nino, the warmer ocean water can drive major changes in global weather patterns.
Scientists and meteorologists classify El Nino as “super” when ocean surface temperatures reach or exceed 2C (3.6F) for a few months. The current El Nino reached 2.7C last month, and some forecasts say it could rise to 4C when it peaks somewhere between November and December.
Why is it so bad this year?
The way El Nino develops depends a lot on “how the atmosphere and the ocean are behaving”, Akshay Deoras, senior research scientist at the University of Reading’s National Centre for Atmospheric Science & Department of Meteorology, told Al Jazeera.
Early in the year generally, “you get winds blowing towards Indonesia and these winds pile up warm water over there. But sometimes, if the winds weaken or the wind pattern is reversed, then that’s when you get strong winds from the Indonesia side, and that leads to a lot of transport of warm water”, Deoras explained.
This warm water then heads towards the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, resulting in El Nino.
“This year, we have really seen these strong winds from Indonesia blowing in the spring season, and they help to transport a large amount of hot water or let’s say warm water, and that’s why we have a super El Nino.”
What effects will it have?
Despite its unprecedented strength, it remains unclear what effects this year’s super El Nino will have on weather around the world.
“Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide,” said Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the United Kingdom’s Met Office.
“Historical evidence shows that El Nino can significantly alter global rainfall patterns,” the Met Office said in a statement.
Regions that often experience reduced rainfall during this period include parts of Central and northern South America, the western Pacific and areas affected by the Indian summer monsoon.
Other areas, including Southern Africa, may face an increased risk of drought.
El Nino also reduces tropical cyclone activity in the Atlantic, with the Met Office adding that no hurricanes have been observed yet this year.
The disruption to rainfall can have severe consequences on global food supplies as agriculture suffers and natural food-growing and harvesting seasons are altered.
Why could El Nino cause so many excess deaths?
The main thing that El Nino does “is it just dumps a lot of heat into the atmosphere and we know that this heat and high temperatures basically supercharges extreme rainfall and weather events”, said Deoras.
A super El Nino not only increases the frequency of these events, but also amplifies their intensity and severity, meaning that there is a “general expectation that we would get more of these extreme weather events across the globe over the next couple of months, and unfortunately, that could translate into a lot of deaths,” said Deoras.
How is climate change involved in this?
Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said that climate change has worsened the impact of El Nino around the world.
“El Nino is likely to bring higher global temperatures and extreme weather impacts in the months ahead, and climate change will further exacerbate these impacts, as the underlying heat driven by fossil fuel emissions continues to push global temperatures higher,” said Otto.
“However, while El Nino patterns are a natural phenomenon that come and go, climate change does not and will only continue to worsen unless we take much faster action globally to move away from fossil fuels.”
Which countries will be worst affected and why?
The Climate Impact Lab report warns that countries in the Global South will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.
The country likely to suffer the most excess heat-related deaths is Nigeria with 31,400, followed by Indonesia with 19,300 and Sudan with 17,600.
Heat in Africa’s Sahel region, including Niger and Chad as well as Nigeria and Sudan, is likely to cause an additional 66,800 deaths.
The researchers also predict that the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia will suffer an additional 19,400 deaths combined.
The number of excess deaths could climb higher if El Nino extends further into next year, with key areas of the Northern Hemisphere, including India and Pakistan, especially vulnerable during their summer months.
Tom Burke, cofounder and director of the climate change think tank E3G, agreed that the Global South would be disproportionately affected.
“Coping with the additional stresses caused by El Nino is harder on countries that have weaker institutions. So the poorer a country it is, the weaker institutions it has,” he told Al Jazeera.
Countries of the Global North, by contrast, have “a whole variety of institutions to respond to these kinds of stresses: fire departments, health systems, etc. They have a quite complex set of institutions to respond to events like this”.
Deoras said added that “it’s quite difficult to” assume that El Nino will impact the Southern Hemisphere

articles.title_orig: Galaxy Tab S12+ and S12 Ultra specs leak - here's what will be upgraded - GSMArena.com news
articles.title_zh: Galaxy Tab S12+ and S12 Ultra specs leak - here's what will be upgraded - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
There has been a slow trickle of leaks for the Galaxy Tab S12+ and Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra. Now, WinFuture has fully opened the tap and... not much came out. The Tab S12 slates will change a few things from their predecessors, but the upgrades are pretty sparse.
Both tablets will be powered by the Dimensity 9500, which replaces a Dimensity 9400+ on the Tab S11 Ultra and a Dimensity 9300+ on the Tab S10+. Why no “plus” chipset this year? Well, MediaTek never released a 9500+ – there is a Dimensity 9600M, but that doesn’t change enough to get a “plus” tag. There’s also the Dimensity 9600 Pro, but that was only just announced. So, Dimensity 9500 it is.
As you may have noticed, the Galaxy Tab S12+ only has one camera on its back – it’s a 13MP wide module. The Tab S10+ did have a dual-camera setup with an 8MP ultra-wide, but Samsung dropped it for some reason.
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra keeps both the 12MP wide and the 8MP ultra-wide modules, plus there is a 12MP selfie. The 14.6” display of the Ultra has a notch to accommodate the selfie camera, while the 12.4” display of the “plus” slate doesn’t need a notch (it has thicker bezels instead).
The Tab S12 Ultra will measure 5.1mm thick (same as before) and will have the same 11,600mAh battery with support for 45W charging. The Tab S12+, however, is getting a new 10,600mAh battery (a minor upgrade from the 10,090mAh of the Tab S10+) with the same 45W charging. The new “plus” slate will be 0.3mm thinner than its predecessor and will measure 5.3mm.
Roland Quandt posted EPREL labels for the two tablets. They show that the batteries are rated for 1,200 charge cycles (no change for the Ultra, but the old “plus” had a 2,000 cycle battery). Also, battery life for the new Ultra has decreased to 88:54h, compared to 94:51h for the 2025 Ultra. As for the “plus” models, the Tab S12+ will last 80:34h, which is an increase from the 73:44h for the Tab S10+. We doubt the 510mAh extra in the battery made that much of a difference, so it’s probably thanks to the more efficient chipset (and possibly screen too).
EPREL labels: Tab S12+ (Wi-Fi) • Tab S12+ (5G) • Tab S12 Ultra (Wi-Fi) • Tab S12 Ultra (5G)
The battery life ratings for the Wi-Fi and 5G versions of the two tablets are the same. Like before, the slates have a low E rating for drop resistance, an average C rating for repairability and an IP68 dust and water resistance rating.
A couple of weeks ago, WinFuture also shared the European prices for the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra and the Tab S12+. Doubling the storage costs €200, while getting a 5G modem is €150 more. For comparison, a Tab S11 Wi-Fi 12/256GB slate started at €1,340 last year, the 5G version with the same storage was €1,490. In other words, the S12 generation Ultra will be €200 more than its predecessor from last year. There was no Tab S11+ last year, so there is no direct comparison.
By the way, we’ve also seen leaks for the US prices and the Indian prices – those leaks showed price hikes of varying degrees. While not officially confirmed, Samsung is expected to unveil the Galaxy Tab S12 series on October 7.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.content_orig:
The months-in-the-making clash between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Benjamin Netanyahu will come to a head on Thursday when the Israeli prime minister delivers a speech before the U.N. General Assembly in Manhattan.
The two are poised to become the focal point of the annual gathering of the world’s most powerful people, which brings motorcades, gridlock and demonstrations to the city. This year’s event comes with an additional layer of drama: During his mayoral campaign last year, Mamdani threatened to arrest Netanyahu on an International Criminal Court warrant. The mayor later clarified he doesn’t have the authority to arrest the prime minister, but has still called him a “war criminal.”
In a CNN interview released on Tuesday, Mamdani maintained his criticism, saying the warrant against Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity is “something that should be honored, because what we want to see, and we’ve been talking about this today, is a faith in our politics, a faith in accountability.”
Netanyahu teased his upcoming remarks on Tuesday with a video where he falsely accused the mayor of supporting Hamas and inciting riots against Jewish New Yorkers. He also delivered a direct message to Mamdani. “I'm coming to the U.N.,” he said. “I'm going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers and I'm going to tell the truth about you.”
Asked about the video, the mayor called Netanyahu the “architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians” and referenced ongoing Israeli attacks in Gaza.
The NYPD has warned protests are anticipated near the U.N. on Manhattan's East Side throughout the General Assembly. Mamdani has said he won’t attend protests against Netanyahu — noting he would uphold the right to demonstrate peacefully.
Sal Albanese, a former city councilmember who advised Mamdani on public safety, said he believed the mayor could balance the two interests of politics and public safety. Mamdani’s pro-Palestinian activism is a key part of his identity that fueled his election and continued popularity, he said. Similarly, protests are a fixture of the city.
“Netanyahu is obviously going to drive a lot of people on the street to protest,” he said. “As long as they do it peacefully, I don’t think it will be a problem.”
In July, Jewish leaders criticized the mayor for inflaming tensions with his criticism of Israel following the stabbings of a Jewish man and an Asian man on the Upper West Side. The attack occurred days after Mamdani had released a video acknowledging that he did not have the legal authority to order Netanyahu’s arrest. Nevertheless, he said Netanyahu was a “war criminal.”
This is not the first time a New York City mayor has clashed with a foreign leader in town for the General Assembly. In 1995, Mayor Rudy Giuliani directed his Chief of Staff Randy Mastro to ask Yasir Arafat, then the chair of the Palestine Liberation Organization, to leave a Lincoln Center concert. The Clinton administration issued a statement criticizing Giuliani’s actions.

articles.title_orig: Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
articles.title_zh: Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
articles.content_orig:
Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
US President Donald Trump has disclosed millions of dollars' worth of stock market trades made during July, including in firms from Elon Musk's SpaceX to tech and AI giants such as Microsoft.
According to official documents, between $6.5m (£4.8m) and $31m worth of stock in Microsoft was sold on behalf of Trump, while they show purchases of between $165,000 and $400,000.
Across more than 1,000 trades, shares were bought and sold in AI company Nvidia and software firm Palantir, a contractor with the US defence department and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the filing shows.
A White House spokesperson said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties.
The spokesperson told the BBC: "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold.
"There are no conflicts of interest."
According to the filing, thousands of dollars' worth of stock was also bought and sold in SpaceX, the rocket, satellite and AI company led by Musk - who was once in charge of the US Department of Government Efficiency.
SpaceX listed its shares on the US-based Nasdaq stock market in June.
Its share price has fluctuated since then, sharply declining in July and August, but it is currently trading 14% higher than its stock market debut.
Shares were also bought and sold in Tesla, Musk's electric vehicle-maker, on behalf of Trump.
Trump has previously publicly disclosed thousands of stock market trades since he returned to the White House in January last year.
The disclosure of the July trades made on behalf of Trump emerged against a backdrop of renewed focus on AI and how safe it is.
Trump has rejected calls for safety-driven slowdowns, warning that restrictions risk the US slipping behind China.
He told an audience of world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that he wants to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" to project American dominance.
Trump has previously argued that the US must come out on top in the AI development race, stating last week: "Whoever wins AI, wins."
He is firmly against government regulation or introducing new guardrails, putting him at odds with many of those gathered at the UN, including Secretary General António Guterres who continues to advocate for binding international safeguards.
The president is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week during a state visit to Washington.
While Trump frames a rebrand as an instrument of national competition, his administration is simultaneously proposing an emergency AI "hotline" with Beijing to manage potential cyber risks or rogue AI incidents.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Citizen Injured After Mistakenly Detained by ICE Near Chicago
articles.title_zh: U.S. Citizen Injured After Mistakenly Detained by ICE Near Chicago
articles.content_orig:
EVANSTON, Ill. (WLS) -- An Evanston man was injured when federal immigration agents detained him after mistakenly believing he was someone they were looking for, according to Evanston police and a witness who recorded part of the confrontation. The man was released after agents determined he was a U.S. citizen.
Miguel Olivares said he was taking a break while helping out at El Pueblito Mexican Grill on Howard Street when he noticed vehicles parked outside and a confrontation unfolding.
"It looked like police vehicles until I started hearing, 'I'm a U.S. citizen. I'm a U.S. citizen,'" Olivares said.
Olivares said he then pulled out his phone and began recording.
"They were being rough with him; they had him pinned against the floor, and it looked like one of the agents hit him in the face," Olivares said.
Evanston police said officers were called to the area Sunday morning after someone reported hearing two men arguing. Officers found an unidentified man on the ground with injuries to his head, neck and teeth and called an ambulance, police said.
Police said witnesses told them the men involved appeared to be U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. Officers later encountered agents nearby who said they were looking for someone who resembled the Evanston man, according to police. The agents determined the man was a U.S. citizen and released him, police said.
The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the individual in question was "not cooperative" with law enforcement.
Olivares said he and others tried to comfort the man after the encounter.
"He was shooken up. He wasn't really able to talk much. All he said was that he was a U.S. citizen, that he doesn't know why they targeted him," Olivares said.
Nathan Ryan of Sanctuary Evanston said the incident warrants accountability and an investigation into the use of force and the mistaken detention of an Evanston resident.
"The only thing that I can think of that's scarier than federal agents beating up people in the street is federal agents beating up people on the street without repercussions," Ryan said.
Evanston's police chief said she met with the victim in the hospital to make sure he has the support he needs. The identities of the Evanston resident and the federal agents have not been released.
A DHS spokesperson said in a statement: "On September 20, during a targeted enforcement operation in Evanston, Illinois, ICE encountered an individual who resembled the target."
"ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself."
"ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself."
"ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use 'reasonable suspicion' to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution."
"The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices."
"DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence."
"We know who we are targeting ahead of time. If and when we do encounter individuals subject to arrest, our law enforcement is trained to ask a series of well-determined questions to determine status and removability."

articles.title_orig: Second man arrested in death of Mississippi woman Tasia Fortune
articles.title_zh: Second man arrested in death of Mississippi woman Tasia Fortune
articles.content_orig:
Jackson police have arrested a second man in the death of Tasia Fortune and obtained an arrest warrant for a third suspect.
Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney announced the arrest during a Tuesday night city council meeting.
NBC affiliate WLBT of Jackson identified the man as Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25.
“What I can tell you is, today, we’ve taken another person into custody and charged them with homicide in this case,” Brackney said.
The U.S. Marshals are assisting with the third warrant.
Fortune, a Black woman, was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned home in Mississippi in August. The case quickly made national headlines and raised concerns because of the state’s history of racially motivated violence and distrust of police handling of death investigations involving Black people.
Over the decades, Mississippi has had more public lynchings than any other state, according to the NAACP, with 581 recorded between 1882 and 1968.
Earlier this month, Jarques Ratliff, 51, was arrested and charged with murder in Fortune’s death. He was denied bond at a court hearing after pleading not guilty.
Both Ratliff and Lloyd are Black. A motive and Fortune’s cause of death have not been released.
Police said Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune but did not release further details.
The Jackson Police Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. It’s unclear whether Lloyd has obtained an attorney.
Brackney said Fortune was found “in a hanging position.”
“And I need to stay with that language as we move this case forward so we do not do anything to jeopardize this case,” she said.
The chief said detectives are pursuing additional warrants for other suspects.
“I will guarantee there are actually more arrests to come in this incident,” she said.
